title: Project 03 · Neural Sequence Laboratory
text:
The idea
You will compare four sequence architectures under one controlled character-level language-modeling setup:

begin with a transparent vanilla RNN on baby names;
replace its recurrent cell with LSTM and GRU cells;
build a small causal Transformer; and
transfer the strongest models from short names to longer recipe text.

Data loading, batching, optimization, evaluation, plotting, and checks are supplied. You implement only the chapter-specific operations that reveal how each architecture works.





flowchart LR
    A[Baby names] --> B[Vanilla RNN]
    B --> C[LSTM + GRU]
    C --> D[Causal Transformer]
    D --> E[Recipe generation]


 The project moves from a controlled short-sequence task to richer long-form generation.

title: Project 01 · The NLP Time Machine
text:
The idea
You will travel through three eras of NLP while solving the same sentiment-classification task:

Rules: write explicit linguistic decisions.
Statistical learning: learn feature weights from labeled examples.
Pretrained Transformers: reuse representations learned from much larger text collections.

The notebook supplies data loading, evaluation, and visualization. You implement a small but meaningful part of every system, receive immediate checks, and finish with a direct comparison on the same 500 SST-2 reviews.





flowchart LR
    A[Rules<br/>3 TODOs] --> B[Statistical model<br/>3 TODOs]
    B --> C[Transformer inference<br/>3 TODOs]
    C --> D[Shared evaluation]
    D --> E[Evidence-based reflection]


 Every era contains student implementation, evaluation, and error analysis.

What you will implement

Era I · Hand-written rules

tokenize() — normalize and extract word tokens while preserving contractions
lexicon_score() — combine positive and negative evidence with simple negation
rule_based_predict() — compose the rule pipeline into a label decision



Era II · Statistical learning

fit_statistical_classifier() — fit unigram/bigram TF–IDF and logistic regression
statistical_predict() — transform new text without leaking test information
strongest_features() — expose the most positive and negative learned weights



Era III · Pretrained Transformer

load_transformer() — load the matching DistilBERT tokenizer and classifier
encode_batch() — create padded, truncated PyTorch inputs
transformer_predict() — compute logits, select classes, and decode labels

title: Lecture Notes Template
text:
1.1 Mathematical typography
A language model assigns a probability to a token sequence. Using the chain rule,
\[
P(w_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(w_i \mid w_{1:i-1}).
\tag{1}\]
Equation 1 should be readable inline with the surrounding explanation. For a bigram approximation,
\[
P(w_i \mid w_{1:i-1}) \approx P(w_i \mid w_{i-1}).
\]






TipIntuition



The chain rule is exact. The approximation appears only when we limit how much history the model may use.

title: Lecture Notes Template
text:
1.2 Code and implementation notes
Code should fit the page, preserve indentation, and remain visually distinct from prose.
from collections import Counter

def unigram_distribution(tokens: list[str]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Estimate a maximum-likelihood unigram distribution."""
    counts = Counter(tokens)
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return {token: count / total for token, count in counts.items()}






WarningCommon mistake



A maximum-likelihood estimate assigns zero probability to every unseen token. Later notes will introduce smoothing and explicit unknown-token handling.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing Chapter 6 · Attention mechanisms
The recurrent encoder–decoder gave us a general recipe for conditional sequence generation: read an input sequence, compress it into a state, and generate an output sequence. Its central weakness was equally simple: every source detail had to cross one fixed-size vector. Attention repairs this bottleneck by allowing a prediction to retrieve information directly from all available source states.
This chapter develops attention as an inspectable soft lookup. We will keep one small translation example visible while deriving scores, weights, and context vectors; then we will reuse the same mechanism inside a single sequence. The chapter ends at the boundary of the Transformer architecture. We will identify what a complete model still needs, but leave the construction of the Transformer block to the next chapter.
flowchart LR
    A[One context<br/>bottleneck] --> B[Soft lookup]
    B --> C[Cross-attention]
    C --> D[Self-attention]
    D --> E[Scale + mask<br/>+ many heads]
    E --> F[Transformer<br/>block?]

    classDef attention fill:#f2e9f7,stroke:#8b5bb5,color:#17364a
    classDef bridge fill:#fff3d6,stroke:#b98a1d,color:#17364a

    class B,C,D,E attention
    class F bridge




Figure 2: Each part keeps the same score–normalize–retrieve operation while changing where queries, keys, and values come from.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 1.1 Recall: one RNN reads, another writes
text:
1.1 Recall: one RNN reads, another writes
Let the source sentence be:
Le colis arrivera demain
and the desired translation be:
The package will arrive tomorrow
An encoder RNN reads the source one token at a time:
\[
h_i=f_{\text{enc}}(h_{i-1},x_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\tag{1}\]
In the simplest recurrent encoder–decoder, only the final state is passed to the decoder:
\[
c=h_n,
\qquad
s_0=c.
\tag{2}\]
The decoder then produces one target state and token distribution at a time:
\[
s_t=f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1},y_{t-1}),
\qquad
p(y_t\mid y_{<t},x)=\operatorname{softmax}(W_o s_t+b_o).
\tag{3}\]

    h1 --> h2[h₂]
    x2[colis] --> h2
    h2 --> h3[h₃]
    x3[arrivera] --> h3
    h3 --> h4[h₄]
    x4[demain] --> h4
    h4 --> c((c))
    c --> s1[s₁]
    s1 --> s2[s₂]
    s2 --> s3[s₃]
    s3 --> s4[s₄]
    s1 --> y1[The]
    s2 --> y2[package]
    s3 --> y3[will arrive]
    s4 --> y4[tomorrow]

    classDef enc fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#356fa8,color:#17364a

Figure 3: The entire source sequence reaches every decoder step through the single context vector \(c=h_4\).





This architecture was historically important: sequence-to-sequence learning showed that a neural model could learn variable-length mappings end to end (Sutskever et al. 2014). The fixed vector, however, forces every source detail—content, order, syntax, entities, and ambiguities—through the same narrow channel.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 1.2 The bottleneck is storage and access
text:
1.2 The bottleneck is storage and access
The problem is often described as insufficient storage: one vector must remember an entire sentence. That is true, but incomplete. Even if a large vector could store every detail, the decoder would still receive the same undifferentiated vector at every output step.



Table 1: Different target predictions need different parts of the source.





Decoder step
Desired output
Most relevant source evidence




1
The
source noun phrase and target syntax


2
package
colis


3
will arrive
arrivera


4
tomorrow
demain






The decoder should not have to unpack the same vector in the same way for every token. It needs an access mechanism: at step \(t\), form a request that selects the source information useful for that prediction.






ImportantThe change in one sentence



Do not discard \(h_1,\ldots,h_n\). Keep every encoder state available, and let each decoder step retrieve a different weighted combination.








flowchart LR
    subgraph Before[Fixed context]
      A1[h₁] --> A4[hₙ]
      A2[h₂] --> A4
      A3[⋯] --> A4
      A4 --> D1[decoder step t]
    end
    subgraph After[Direct access]
      B1[h₁] --> C[weighted context cₜ]
      B2[h₂] --> C
      B3[⋯] --> C
      B4[hₙ] --> C
      Q[decoder request sₜ₋₁] --> C
      C --> D2[predict yₜ]
    end

    classDef old fill:#f8e5df,stroke:#d95f43,color:#17364a

Figure 4: Attention replaces one mandatory path through \(h_n\) with direct, prediction-dependent access to all encoder memories.





Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio introduced this learned alignment mechanism for neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al. 2015). Luong, Pham, and Manning later systematized several global and local variants (Luong et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
1.3 Section synthesis
The recurrent encoder–decoder compresses because it discards intermediate states. Attention begins with a simple reversal of that decision: preserve the states and learn how to access them.
The next question is computational: how can a model select one memory while remaining differentiable end to end?

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.1 Keep every source memory
After encoding four tokens, retain the matrix of source states:
\[
H=
\begin{bmatrix}
h_1^\top\\
h_2^\top\\
h_3^\top\\
h_4^\top
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times d_h}.
\tag{4}\]
At decoder step \(t\), the previous decoder state \(s_{t-1}\) summarizes what has already been generated. It therefore acts as a request. Informally:

“Given what I have translated so far, which source memory should influence the next word?”

A hard lookup would choose one index \(i\). That discrete choice is awkward to train with ordinary backpropagation. Attention instead performs a soft lookup: assign every memory a nonnegative weight, make the weights sum to one, and retrieve their weighted average.






flowchart LR
    Q[request<br/>query q] --> S{compare}
    K1[key k₁] --> S
    K2[key k₂] --> S
    K3[key k₃] --> S
    S --> W[weights α₁, α₂, α₃]
    V1[value v₁] --> C[weighted sum c]
    V2[value v₂] --> C
    V3[value v₃] --> C
    W --> C

    classDef query fill:#f8e5df,stroke:#d95f43,color:#17364a
    classDef memory fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#356fa8,color:#17364a
    classDef operation fill:#f2e9f7,stroke:#8b5bb5,color:#17364a
    class Q query
    class K1,K2,K3,V1,V2,V3 memory
    class S,W,C operation




Figure 5: A query compares with every key; normalized weights determine how much of every value is retrieved.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.2 Three operations: score, normalize, retrieve
For a query \(q\) and memory pairs \((k_i,v_i)\):

Score each query–key pair:
\[
e_i=\operatorname{score}(q,k_i).
\tag{5}\]
Normalize all scores with softmax:
\[
\alpha_i=\frac{\exp(e_i)}{\sum_j\exp(e_j)}.
\tag{6}\]
Retrieve a weighted combination of values:
\[
c=\sum_i \alpha_i v_i.
\tag{7}\]

The weights satisfy \(\alpha_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\). The context is therefore a convex combination of values.






ImportantPause · exact calculation



Suppose one query produces the scores
\[
e=[1,3,0,2]
\]
for four scalar values
\[
v=[2,5,-1,3].
\]

Calculate \(\alpha=\operatorname{softmax}(e)\).
Calculate \(c=\sum_i\alpha_i v_i\).
Which value contributes most, and why?

Implement softmax after subtracting the maximum score:

\]

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.4 What learning changes
No human assigns the scores in Table 2. The scoring parameters are trained through the final task loss. If attending to demain helps predict tomorrow, backpropagation adjusts the projections so that similar query–key pairs receive larger scores in future examples.
The attention weights are intermediate differentiable variables:

    A --> C[context c]
    C --> Y[next-token distribution]
    Y --> L[loss]

    Y -. gradient .-> C
    C -. gradient .-> A
    A -. gradient .-> E
    E -. gradient .-> P

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.5 Section synthesis
Attention is not a mysterious new memory type. It is a differentiable retrieval rule:
\[
\boxed{\text{score} \rightarrow \text{normalize} \rightarrow \text{retrieve}}.
\]
We have not yet specified what the query, keys, and values represent. Cross-attention gives those roles a concrete meaning in translation.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 3.1 Queries, keys, and values are roles
text:
3.1 Queries, keys, and values are roles
In encoder–decoder attention:



Table 3: The same source state can be projected once as a key and once as a value.










Role
Comes from
Question answered




Query \(q_t\)
current or previous decoder state
What information is needed now?


Keys \(k_i\)
encoder states
Which source position matches the request?


Values \(v_i\)
encoder states
What content should be retrieved?






A common projected form is
\[
q_t=s_{t-1}W_Q,
\qquad
k_i=h_iW_K,
\qquad
v_i=h_iW_V.
\tag{8}\]
The key and value originate from the same source state but serve different purposes. A useful analogy is a library:

the key is the catalog description used to decide relevance;
the value is the book content retrieved after the match.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
3.2 Scoring functions
Several differentiable compatibility functions are possible.

3.2.1 Dot product
\[
e_{ti}=q_t^\top k_i.
\tag{9}\]
Dot products are efficient and become the standard form in the Transformer.


3.2.2 Additive attention
\[
e_{ti}=v_a^\top\tanh(W_q q_t+W_k k_i+b_a).
\tag{10}\]
This small neural network was used in the original alignment model (Bahdanau et al. 2015). Additive and multiplicative variants can learn similar behaviors, but their dimensions, parameter counts, and computational profiles differ (Luong et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 3.4 A new query creates a new alignment
text:
3.4 A new query creates a new alignment
When the decoder moves from package to will arrive to tomorrow, the source keys and values stay fixed, but the query changes. Therefore the attention distribution changes:
\[
\alpha_t
=
\operatorname{softmax}(q_tK^\top).
\tag{13}\]



Table 5: Cross-attention is conditional retrieval, not one global sentence summary.





Target step
Query intent
Likely strongest source key




package
retrieve the translated entity
colis


will arrive
retrieve the event
arrivera


tomorrow
retrieve the time expression
demain






An attention matrix places one decoder query on each row and one source key on each column. Heatmaps of this matrix can reveal plausible alignments, diffuse uncertainty, repeated coverage, or systematic errors.






WarningAn attention heatmap is evidence—not a proof of reasoning



Weights show how values are mixed at a particular attention operation. They do not, by themselves, establish a complete causal explanation of the model prediction. Alternative weight patterns can sometimes produce similar outputs (Jain and Wallace 2019). Use heatmaps as diagnostic evidence together with interventions, errors, and other analyses.

title: Attention Mechanisms
Attention Mechanisms
section: 4.1 Change the origin, keep the mechanism
text:
4.1 Change the origin, keep the mechanism
Cross-attention and self-attention use the same score–normalize–retrieve rule. Only the source of the roles changes.



Table 6: Attention is named by where its roles originate.











Mechanism
Queries
Keys
Values




Cross-attention
target/decoder sequence
source/encoder sequence
source/encoder sequence


Self-attention
one sequence
the same sequence
the same sequence






For an input matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{model}}\),
\[
Q=XW_Q,
\qquad
K=XW_K,
\qquad
V=XW_V.
\tag{14}\]
The same token vector therefore produces three different learned views: what it asks for, how it advertises itself for matching, and what content it offers if selected.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 4.3 Every token asks its own question
text:
4.3 Every token asks its own question
Self-attention does not only contextualize the pronoun. Every position \(i\) supplies its own query \(q_i\), produces its own distribution over all keys, and receives its own output \(z_i\):
\[
z_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{ij}v_j.
\tag{16}\]
All \(n^2\) scores can be computed together:
\[
S=QK^\top
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
\tag{17}\]
\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{row}(S),
\qquad
Z=AV.
\tag{18}\]
For our seven-token sentence, the dimensions are inspectable:

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
4.4 Shorter paths and parallel computation
In a recurrent network, information from position 2 to position 6 crosses four sequential state updates. In one self-attention layer, a learned edge can connect those positions directly.



Table 8: Self-attention changes both the information path and the computational trade-off.










Property
Recurrent layer
Self-attention layer




Long-range path length
grows with distance
one attention edge


Training across positions
sequential
parallel matrix operations


Pairwise interaction cost
linear per recurrent step
quadratic in sequence length


Explicit notion of order
recurrence provides it
must be supplied separately






The quadratic \(n\times n\) score matrix is powerful but can become expensive for very long sequences. This limitation motivates later work on sparse, local, linear, and memory-efficient attention. It does not change the basic lookup derived here.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
4.5 Section synthesis
Self-attention creates direct, context-dependent token representations and evaluates all queries in parallel. Two practical questions remain:

Why do dot products become unstable as vector width grows?
How can a language model prevent a position from reading future tokens?

A third modeling question will follow: can one attention distribution capture every useful relation?

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
5.1 Why scale dot products?
Consider a query and key with four matching coordinates:
\[
q=[1,1,1,1],
\qquad
k=[1,1,1,1].
\]
Their dot product is
\[
q^\top k=1+1+1+1=4.
\]
With wider random vectors, more products are summed. Under common independence assumptions, if query and key coordinates have mean zero and variance one, the dot product has variance proportional to \(d_k\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(q^\top k)=d_k.
\]
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) restores an approximately unit variance:
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{q^\top k}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\approx1.
\]
This matters because large logits make softmax extremely sharp. Probabilities approach zero or one, where useful gradients may become small (Vaswani et al. 2017).






ImportantPause · compare two distributions



Given scores \([4,2,0]\) and \(d_k=4\), compare:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}([4,2,0])
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{[4,2,0]}{\sqrt4}\right).
\]
Which distribution leaves more probability for alternatives?

text:
5.2 Worked scaling example
Since \(\sqrt{d_k}=2\), the scaled scores are \([2,1,0]\).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 5.3 Causal masking: do not read tomorrow
text:
5.3 Causal masking: do not read tomorrow
Suppose an autoregressive language model is trained on:
The animal ran home
At position 3, the task is to predict the next token home from the prefix The animal ran. Unrestricted self-attention would allow the query at position 3 to inspect position 4, leaking the answer.
The causal rule is:
\[
\text{query position }i\text{ may attend to key position }j
\quad\text{only if}\quad j\le i.
\tag{20}\]
Define an additive mask \(M\):
\[
M_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
0, & j\le i,\\
-\infty, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\tag{21}\]
For four positions:

The masked operation is
\[
\widetilde S
=
\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M,
\]
\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{row}(\widetilde S),
\qquad
Z=AV.
\tag{22}\]
Because \(\exp(-\infty)=0\), every forbidden future weight becomes zero. All positions can still be processed in parallel during training; the mask controls information, not execution order.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
5.4 Why use multiple heads?
Consider:

The animal did not cross the street because it was wide.

For the token it, several relations may be useful:

reference: it \(\rightarrow\) street;
description: it \(\rightarrow\) wide;
event participants: cross \(\rightarrow\) animal, street.

A single head produces one attention distribution per query. It can mix several signals, but a multi-head layer provides distinct learned projection spaces:
\[
head_r
=
\operatorname{Attention}(QW_r^Q,KW_r^K,VW_r^V),
\tag{23}\]
\[
\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{Concat}(head_1,\ldots,head_h)W^O.
\tag{24}\]

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
5.5 Reading attention visualizations
Two common views are useful.

5.5.1 Attention heatmap
Rows represent queries, columns represent keys, and color intensity represents \(\alpha_{ij}\). A heatmap is effective for inspecting all pairwise weights in one head.


5.5.2 Connection view
Tokens are connected by lines whose opacity or width represents attention strength. This view makes a small number of strong relations visually immediate.
BertViz provides head, model, and neuron-oriented views for Transformer attention (Vig 2019). For a research example connecting heads with linguistic relations, read Clark et al., What Does BERT Look At? (Clark et al. 2019).






WarningInterpret with care



An attractive attention line is not automatically the reason for a prediction. Inspect:

several heads and layers, not one selected picture;
whether the pattern is stable across examples;
how changing or removing attended tokens changes the output;
whether value vectors and downstream layers preserve the apparent relation; and
whether another attention distribution produces a similar result.

Attention visualization is a valuable microscope, not a complete theory of model reasoning (Jain and Wallace 2019).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
5.6 Modern attention in one view



Table 11: Three additions that form the modern attention operator.










Mechanism
Operation
Problem addressed




Scaling
divide logits by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)
softmax saturation as width grows


Causal mask
add \(-\infty\) above the diagonal
future-token leakage


Multiple heads
parallel projected lookups
reliance on one similarity space






The operator is now stable, information-valid, and able to learn several views. It is still not a complete sequence model.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 6.1 Self-attention has no order by itself
text:
6.1 Self-attention has no order by itself
Compare:
dog bites man
man bites dog
The token set is the same, but the meanings differ. If \(P\) is a permutation matrix that reorders positions, self-attention without positional information is permutation equivariant:
\[
\operatorname{Attn}(PX)
=
P\operatorname{Attn}(X).
\tag{25}\]
Reordering inputs merely reorders outputs. The operation has no independent signal that position 1 came before position 3. A sequence architecture must therefore inject position information. The next chapter will compare ways to do so.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: 6.2 Attention mixes positions, not features deeply
text:
6.2 Attention mixes positions, not features deeply
Attention answers:

Which positions should exchange information?

After that exchange, each token also needs a nonlinear transformation of its features:

How should this position transform the information it received?

One attention layer creates one round of interaction. Rich models stack many layers, which raises two questions:

Can an original representation survive repeated transformations?
Can activation and gradient scales remain controlled across depth?

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Chapter 4 · Statistical language modeling
When a phone proposes the next word, a search engine completes a query, or a speech recognizer compares possible transcriptions, the system needs a distribution over what may come next. A language model supplies that distribution.
This chapter develops the smallest useful language model from first principles. We will keep one corpus visible, inspect every count, and follow the model through prediction, generation, smoothing, and evaluation. Its failures will then create the question that motivates recurrent neural networks.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
1.1 Greedy choice versus sampling
Two common decision rules use the same distribution differently.
Greedy decoding selects the most probable word:
\[
\hat w=\underset{w\in V}{\arg\max}\;P(w\mid h).
\tag{1}\]
For Table 1, greedy decoding always selects language.
Sampling draws a word according to the entire categorical distribution. One implementation partitions \([0,1)\) into cumulative intervals:
language     [0.00, 0.40)
statistics   [0.40, 0.70)
together     [0.70, 0.85)
other        [0.85, 1.00)
If \(r=0.58\), the sampled word is statistics. Sampling can therefore choose a less likely continuation without pretending it was the most likely one.






TipPrediction is not generation



Prediction performs one next-word decision. Generation repeats prediction, appends the selected word, and uses the enlarged sequence as the next history.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
2.1 The Markov approximation
An n-gram model deliberately keeps only a fixed suffix of the history:
\[
P(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1})
\approx
P(w_t\mid w_{t-n+1:t-1}).
\tag{3}\]

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
3.2 Maximum-likelihood estimation
The relative-frequency or maximum-likelihood estimate is
\[
P_{\text{MLE}}(w\mid h)=\frac{C(h,w)}{C(h)}.
\tag{5}\]
The numerator counts the requested transition. The denominator counts every occasion on which the history had an opportunity to transition to something.
For the history study,
\[
P(language\mid study)=\frac{3}{5}=0.60,
\qquad
P(statistics\mid study)=\frac{2}{5}=0.40.
\]
These values form a complete row:
\[
\sum_wP(w\mid study)=0.60+0.40=1.
\]






WarningCommon denominator error



Do not divide \(C(study,language)\) by the total number of corpus tokens. A conditional probability row is normalized by the number of occurrences of its history, \(C(study)\).








ImportantCheckpoint · recover the counts first



Using the visible corpus, calculate:

\(P(study\mid students)\);
\(P(language\mid study)\); and
\(P(statistics\mid study)\).

For every result, write \(C(h,w)\) and \(C(h)\) before dividing.








NoteWorked solution





\[
P(study\mid students)
=\frac{C(students,study)}{C(students)}
=\frac34=0.75.
\]
\[
P(language\mid study)
=\frac{C(study,language)}{C(study)}
=\frac35=0.60.
\]
\[
P(statistics\mid study)
=\frac{C(study,statistics)}{C(study)}
=\frac25=0.40.
\]

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
3.3 A direct implementation
The implementation should preserve the same inspectable objects as the calculation.
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

sentences = [
    ["students", "study", "language"],
    ["students", "study", "statistics"],
    ["researchers", "study", "language"],
    ["students", "learn", "statistics"],
    ["researchers", "study", "statistics"],
    ["students", "study", "language"],
]

bigram_counts = defaultdict(Counter)
history_counts = Counter()

for sentence in sentences:
    tokens = ["<s>", *sentence, "</s>"]
    for history, word in zip(tokens, tokens[1:]):
        bigram_counts[history][word] += 1
        history_counts[history] += 1

def mle_probability(word: str, history: str) -> float:
    numerator = bigram_counts[history][word]
    denominator = history_counts[history]
    return numerator / denominator if denominator else 0.0
This code stores a sparse map instead of allocating every possible vocabulary pair. That choice matters because a vocabulary of size \(|V|\) permits \(|V|^2\) bigram cells.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
4.1 Greedy generation
Starting at <s>, a greedy decoder follows the largest value in every row:
<s> --students (.67)--> students --study (.75)--> study
    --language (.60)--> language --</s> (1.00)--> stop
With fixed probabilities and no ties, repeating greedy decoding from the same start state produces the same sentence every time.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
4.2 Sampling generation
A sampler may follow the same first steps but choose statistics from the study row with probability \(0.40\):
<s> → students → study → statistics → </s>
Sampling increases variety, but it also permits lower-probability and occasionally poor paths. Temperature and top-\(k\)/top-\(p\) methods refine this trade-off in modern neural generation; the fundamental distinction remains whether we maximize or draw from the distribution (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
4.3 Scoring a complete sentence
The bigram approximation assigns
\[
P(w_{1:n})
\approx P(w_1\mid\langle s\rangle)
\prod_{t=2}^{n}P(w_t\mid w_{t-1})
P(\langle/ s\rangle\mid w_n).
\tag{6}\]
For students study language, our corpus gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(&\text{students study language})
&=P(students\mid\langle s\rangle)
  P(study\mid students)\\
&\quad\times P(language\mid study)
  P(\langle/ s\rangle\mid language)\\
&=\frac46\times\frac34\times\frac35\times\frac33\\
&=0.30.
\end{aligned}
\]
Longer sequences multiply more numbers below one, so their raw probabilities naturally become smaller.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
4.4 Log-probabilities prevent numerical underflow
Multiplying hundreds of small floating-point values can underflow toward zero. Taking logarithms converts products into sums:
\[
\log P(w_{1:n})=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\log P(w_t\mid h_t).
\tag{7}\]
Because logarithm is monotonic, the sequence with the largest probability also has the largest log-probability.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
6.1 Add-one smoothing
The clearest introductory rule adds one pseudo-count to every candidate:
\[
P_{+1}(w\mid h)
=\frac{C(h,w)+1}{C(h)+|V|}.
\tag{8}\]
The denominator adds \(|V|\) because one pseudo-count was added to each of the \(|V|\) possible continuations.
If \(C(study)=4\), \(C(study,together)=0\), and \(|V|=4\), then
\[
P_{+1}(together\mid study)
=\frac{0+1}{4+4}
=0.125.
\]
Add-one smoothing makes the logic inspectable, but for large word vocabularies it usually removes too much mass from observed events. It is therefore mainly a teaching baseline, not a strong practical word-level language model (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3; Chen and Goodman 1999).

Figure 10: The observations do not change. Only the estimated probability table becomes dense.











WarningPrecise wording matters



The count matrix remains sparse: smoothing does not hallucinate corpus events. The estimated probability matrix becomes dense because formerly unseen events receive small positive probabilities.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
6.3 Better smoothing families
Practical n-gram models use the structure of the count distribution more carefully.

Backoff uses a lower-order model when the detailed history has weak or missing evidence. Katz’s influential method combines discounting with backoff (Katz 1987).
Interpolation mixes estimates from several orders instead of selecting only one.
Kneser–Ney smoothing discounts observed counts and uses a continuation distribution that rewards words appearing after many distinct histories (Kneser and Ney 1995).

For example, an interpolated trigram model may use
\[
P(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})
=\lambda_3P_{\text{tri}}(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})
+\lambda_2P_{\text{bi}}(w_t\mid w_{t-1})
+\lambda_1P_{\text{uni}}(w_t),
\]
where \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1\).

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
7.1 Average negative log-probability
For a test sequence of \(N\) predicted tokens, the average negative log-probability is
\[
H(W)=-\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log_2P(w_t\mid h_t).
\tag{9}\]
This quantity measures average surprise in bits. A confident correct prediction contributes little surprise; assigning a tiny probability to the observed word contributes much more.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
7.2 Perplexity
Perplexity exponentiates the average surprise:
\[
\operatorname{PP}(W)
=2^{H(W)}
=P(w_{1:N})^{-1/N}.
\tag{10}\]
Equivalently, using natural logarithms,
\[
\operatorname{PP}(W)
=\exp\left(-\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log P(w_t\mid h_t)\right).
\]
Lower perplexity means the model assigns more probability, on average, to the observed held-out tokens (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
7.3 A fully visible calculation
Suppose a test sequence produces four conditional probabilities:
\[
\frac12,\quad\frac14,\quad\frac12,\quad 1.
\]
Their product is
\[
P(W)=\frac12\times\frac14\times\frac12\times1=\frac1{16}.
\]
With \(N=4\) predicted tokens,
\[
\operatorname{PP}(W)
=\left(\frac1{16}\right)^{-1/4}
=16^{1/4}
=2.
\]
The model behaves as though it faces two equally plausible choices at each position on average. This “effective branching factor” is an intuition, not a literal claim that every row contains exactly two words.






ImportantCheckpoint · compare two models



Model A has test perplexity \(2.1\) and Model B has test perplexity \(3.4\). Which model better predicts the test text? What additional information is required before the comparison is valid?








NoteWorked answer





Model A has the lower average held-out surprise. The comparison is valid only if both values use the same test text, tokenization, vocabulary, unknown-word policy, and treatment of boundary tokens. Perplexities computed under different tokenizations are not directly comparable.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
7.4 Perplexity is intrinsic, not final
Perplexity measures the language model itself. An application ultimately needs an extrinsic metric:



Table 6: Intrinsic improvements are valuable only when they support the real task.









Application
Example downstream measure




Autocomplete
suggestion acceptance rate


Speech recognition
word error rate


Machine translation
human judgments or translation-quality metric


Text generation
task success, factuality, safety, and human preference

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
8.1 A bigram remembers one token
Consider:

The keys to the cabinet ___

English agreement favors are because the subject keys is plural. A bigram model sees only cabinet → ?; the relevant cue has disappeared.






flowchart LR
    K[keys<br/>plural cue] --> T[to]
    T --> D[the]
    D --> C[cabinet<br/>bigram history]
    C --> Q[is or are?]
    K -. "dependency the bigram cannot retain" .-> Q

    classDef cue fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef local fill:#fff3d6,stroke:#b98a1d,color:#17364a
    classDef decision fill:#f8e5df,stroke:#d95f43,color:#17364a
    class K cue
    class C local
    class Q decision




Figure 12: The predictive cue can lie outside a fixed n-gram window.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
section: 8.2 Increasing the order makes the table explode
text:
8.2 Increasing the order makes the table explode
With a vocabulary of \(50{,}000\) tokens:
\[
|V|^2=2.5\text{ billion possible bigrams},
\]
\[
|V|^3=125\text{ trillion possible trigrams}.
\]
Most possible n-grams are never observed. Raising \(n\) extends memory but worsens parameter growth and sparsity.

title: Statistical Language Modeling
text:
8.3 Similar words cannot share counts
Suppose the corpus contains:
students   → study    observed 12 times
researchers → study   observed 9 times
pupils     → study    observed 0 times
Even if students and pupils are semantically similar, the n-gram table treats their transitions as unrelated entries. Evidence collected for one symbol does not automatically improve the other.



Table 7: Four pressures that motivate learned, distributed sequence representations.





Limitation
Observable symptom




Fixed memory
distant cues disappear


Parameter growth
\(|V|^n\) possible n-grams


Sparsity
most entries remain unobserved


No distributed sharing
similar words use separate counts

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Optional reference · Detailed text processing

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
1.1 What makes language difficult?
Language is productive, context-dependent, and ambiguous. The same surface form can support several analyses, while different surface forms can express nearly the same intent. Consider:

I saw the student with the telescope.

The prepositional phrase with the telescope can describe the instrument used for seeing, or the student who possessed the telescope. Nothing about splitting the sentence at spaces resolves that structural ambiguity.
Ambiguity appears at several interacting levels:



Table 1: Linguistic levels are analytical lenses, not independent processing boxes.










Level
Central question
Example




Morphology
How are meaningful pieces combined inside a word?
un-help-ful-ness


Syntax
Which words form constituents and dependencies?
Who has the telescope?


Semantics
What entities, events, and relations are expressed?
bank as an institution or river edge


Pragmatics
What does the speaker intend in context?
“Can you open the window?” as a request


Discourse
How do sentences connect across a text?
What does it refer to?












flowchart LR
    P[Pragmatic and social context]
    D[Discourse context]
    S[Sentence structure]
    W[Word form]
    O[Observed characters]
    P --> D --> S --> W --> O




Figure 2: Interpretation is constrained by nested sources of context.





Table 1 and Figure 2 should not be read as a fixed recipe in which morphology always runs before syntax. Modern models often learn several levels jointly. The useful lesson is that a visible string underdetermines its interpretation. Text processing must therefore preserve distinctions relevant to the eventual task.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
section: 1.2 A task changes what counts as signal
text:
1.2 A task changes what counts as signal
Suppose the input is:

AMAZING service!!! 😍😍

For topic classification, case and repeated punctuation may be dispensable. For sentiment or author-style analysis, they are evidence. For a moderation system, the emoji may be crucial. There is no universally “clean” version of this sentence; there are only transformations justified—or not justified—by a task.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
3.1 Bytes and encodings
A byte is an integer from 0 to 255. Files and network messages are byte sequences. An encoding specifies how those bytes represent text. UTF-8 is the dominant Unicode encoding on the web and uses one to four bytes per code point. ASCII characters keep their familiar one-byte values, while other characters use multibyte sequences (Jurafsky and Martin 2026).
Decoding must precede linguistic processing:
payload = b"caf\xc3\xa9"
text = payload.decode("utf-8")
assert text == "café"
Using the wrong encoding can produce an error or mojibake: valid-looking but corrupted text such as cafÃ©. Once corruption is silently accepted and the original bytes are discarded, recovery may be ambiguous.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
section: 3.2 Code points are not necessarily visible characters
text:
3.2 Code points are not necessarily visible characters
Unicode assigns an abstract integer called a code point to each encoded character. Python’s ord() exposes that integer:
for char in "NLP":
    print(char, f"U+{ord(char):04X}")
N U+004E
L U+004C
P U+0050
But a visible symbol can contain several code points. The decomposed spelling e followed by COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT is perceived as one é. Emoji sequences make this distinction even clearer: a family emoji can contain several people joined by ZERO WIDTH JOINER characters.
Unicode calls a user-perceived unit an extended grapheme cluster and specifies default grapheme, word, and sentence boundary rules in Unicode Standard Annex #29 (Unicode Consortium 2025b). These rules are essential for cursor motion, truncation, and display, but they do not by themselves define the linguistic tokens required by every NLP task.






TipA practical debugging habit



When two strings look equal but compare unequal, inspect repr(text), the code points, and the Unicode names before blaming the model.


import unicodedata

def inspect_text(text: str) -> None:
    for char in text:
        print(
            f"U+{ord(char):04X}",
            unicodedata.name(char, "<unnamed>"),
            repr(char),
        )

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
4.1 Canonical decomposition and composition
For many accented characters, Unicode permits both:

a precomposed code point: é = U+00E9;
a decomposed sequence: e + ◌́ = U+0065 U+0301.

The normalization forms differ along two axes:



Table 2: The four Unicode normalization forms. The K marks compatibility normalization.





Form
Equivalence used
Result




NFD
Canonical
Decomposed


NFC
Canonical
Decomposed, then recomposed where possible


NFKD
Compatibility
Decomposed


NFKC
Compatibility
Decomposed, then recomposed where possible












flowchart LR
    A[Input text] --> B{Which equivalence?}
    B -->|canonical| C[NFD<br/>decompose]
    B -->|compatibility| D[NFKD<br/>decompose more distinctions]
    C --> E[NFC<br/>compose]
    D --> F[NFKC<br/>compose]




Figure 5: Canonical and compatibility normalization answer different questions.





NFC is a sensible default for much stored natural-language text: it respects canonical equivalence while usually retaining compact composed forms. Python implements the standard operation directly:
import unicodedata

left = "café"             # U+00E9
right = "cafe\N{COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT}"

assert left != right
assert unicodedata.normalize("NFC", left) == unicodedata.normalize("NFC", right)

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
4.3 Normalization is not “remove everything unusual”
Lowercasing, accent removal, punctuation deletion, whitespace collapsing, and Unicode normalization are separate operations. Each has different semantics. Consider Turkish I, İ, ı, and i; case operations are language-sensitive. Consider Arabic diacritics: removing them may reduce sparsity but can also erase lexical or grammatical information. A robust system names each transformation rather than hiding them inside a function called clean_text.
The order also matters. A useful pipeline records it explicitly:
from dataclasses import dataclass
import re
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class NormalizationPolicy:
    unicode_form: str = "NFC"
    collapse_whitespace: bool = True
    casefold: bool = False

def normalize_text(text: str, policy: NormalizationPolicy) -> str:
    result = unicodedata.normalize(policy.unicode_form, text)
    if policy.casefold:
        result = result.casefold()
    if policy.collapse_whitespace:
        result = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", result).strip()
    return result
This code is intentionally conservative. It does not delete punctuation, strip accents, or guess at malformed encodings.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
5.1 Tokenization is a contract
Before implementing a tokenizer, state the contract:

Task: What will consume the tokens?
Domain: News, source code, clinical notes, social media, or legal text?
Languages and scripts: Which writing systems and orthographic conventions occur?
Protected spans: Should URLs, email addresses, numbers, or emoji remain intact?
Reversibility: Must tokens reconstruct the original string?
Alignment: Must predictions map back to exact source offsets?







flowchart LR
    A[Raw span] --> B{Protected pattern?}
    B -->|URL, email, date| C[Keep as one span]
    B -->|no| D{Language-specific rule?}
    D -->|contraction or clitic| E[Split or preserve by policy]
    D -->|no| F{Punctuation boundary?}
    F -->|yes| G[Emit separate punctuation]
    F -->|no| H[Continue scanning]
    C --> I[Token + start/end offsets]
    E --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I




Figure 6: Tokenization turns a task specification into explicit boundary decisions.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
section: 5.2 The same sentence supports different valid tokenizations
text:
5.2 The same sentence supports different valid tokenizations
Consider I can't visit New York.:








Purpose
Possible tokens
Reason




Surface display
I, can't, visit, New, York, .
Preserve familiar written words


Syntactic analysis
I, ca, n't, visit, New, York, .
Expose the negation clitic


Named-entity model
I, can, ', t, visit, New, York, .
Model-specific vocabulary rules


Gazetteer lookup
I, can't, visit, New York, .
Preserve a multiword entity candidate



None is universally correct. Correctness is measured against the declared contract and downstream behavior.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
5.3 Offsets make tokens useful
A production token should usually store its source interval:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    text: str
    start: int
    end: int

source = "NLP is fun!"
token = Token(text="NLP", start=0, end=3)
assert source[token.start:token.end] == token.text
Offsets support highlighting, annotation, debugging, and error analysis. If normalization changes string length, offsets in the normalized text no longer automatically identify the same positions in the source. Preserve the original or maintain an alignment map.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
5.4 A preview of subword tokenization
Word vocabularies face an open-vocabulary problem: new names, inflections, compounds, and spelling variants appear continually. Character models avoid unknown words but create long sequences. Subword tokenization occupies the space between them, representing frequent strings as single units and rarer strings as compositions.
Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch adapted byte-pair encoding (BPE) for neural machine translation, showing that rare words can be modeled as subword sequences rather than mapped to a single unknown token (Sennrich et al. 2016). The broader history includes characters, morphemes, learned subwords, and bytes; no granularity is optimal for all applications (Mielke et al. 2021).






flowchart LR
    A[Bytes or characters<br/>tiny vocabulary<br/>long sequences]
    B[Subwords<br/>open vocabulary<br/>moderate sequences]
    C[Words<br/>large vocabulary<br/>short sequences]
    A <-- finer units --> B
    B <-- coarser units --> C




Figure 7: Token granularity trades sequence length against vocabulary size and lexical coverage.





Tokenizers can also distribute capacity unevenly across languages. Controlled experiments found that replacing a multilingual model’s tokenizer with a language-specialized tokenizer improved downstream performance for almost every studied language/task combination (Rust et al. 2021). We will return to BPE, WordPiece, and model vocabularies when we study pretrained language models. For now, retain the key idea: a tokenizer is part of the model.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
section: 6.1 Why \w+ is not a universal tokenizer
text:
6.1 Why \w+ is not a universal tokenizer
In Python string patterns, \w is Unicode-aware and includes Unicode alphanumeric characters plus underscore, unless ASCII-only behavior is requested (Python Software Foundation 2026). That is useful, but “Unicode alphanumeric” is not equivalent to “word in every language.” It does not encode task-specific policies for apostrophes, emoji sequences, URLs, or clitics.
A small scanner can combine protected patterns with a fallback rule:
import re

TOKEN_PATTERN = re.compile(
    r"""
    https?://[^\s]+                  # URL candidate
    |[\w.+-]+@[\w.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,} # email candidate
    |\w+(?:['’]\w+)*                 # word with apostrophes
    |[^\w\s]                         # one punctuation/symbol
    """,
    re.VERBOSE | re.UNICODE,
)

def regex_tokenize(text: str) -> list[Token]:
    return [Token(m.group(), m.start(), m.end()) for m in TOKEN_PATTERN.finditer(text)]
This is a teaching tokenizer, not a universal one. Its URL rule may absorb trailing punctuation; its email grammar is incomplete; and its treatment of emoji is naïve. Those limitations should become tests, not footnotes we forget.






WarningRegex has a scope



Use regex when the pattern is local and the accepted language can be described clearly. Use a tokenizer or parser when decisions require extensive linguistic context, nested structure, or maintained language-specific rules.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
7.1 Compare tokenizers with adversarial examples
A useful evaluation set is small, diverse, and difficult on purpose:
CASES = [
    "I can't attend.",
    "Email nlp@example.org.",
    "Version 3.10.18 is installed.",
    "رائع جدًا!",
    "中文分词并不依赖空格。",
    "👩🏽‍💻 builds NLP systems.",
]
For each example, inspect:

token strings;
start and end offsets;
reconstruction of the original;
behavior of protected spans;
stability under the chosen normalization policy; and
suitability for the downstream task.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
8.2 Keep policy separate from mechanism
The function implementing normalization is a mechanism. Whether to case-fold is policy. Separating them makes experiments comparable and prevents an undocumented change from silently altering the dataset.
A minimal experiment record might include:
preprocessing:
  encoding: utf-8
  unicode_normalization: NFC
  casefold: false
  tokenizer: regex-tokenizer-v1
  preserve_offsets: true
Version the policy with the code and tests. A project manager such as uv can lock Python dependencies, but a lockfile alone does not record preprocessing choices.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
9.1 Step 1: preserve and inspect
Store the exact source. Inspect unexpected code points. The full-width digits ５０ are compatibility variants, and the emoji contains multiple code points. Neither fact is visible from a whitespace split.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
9.2 Step 2: choose a normalization view

NFC safely regularizes canonical composition.
NFKC would turn ５０ into 50, which may help a price feature.
Case-folding AMAZING would remove emphasis that could be useful for sentiment.
Deleting Arabic text because a Latin-oriented rule does not recognize it would be data loss, not cleaning.

A defensible design preserves the NFC source view and derives a separate NFKC search/feature view when needed.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
9.3 Step 3: tokenize with protected spans
The email should remain one candidate. Repeated exclamation marks may be stored separately or as a run, but the policy should preserve the count if emphasis matters. The emoji should be segmented using grapheme-aware tooling if the application treats it as one visible unit.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
9.4 Step 4: retain evidence
For every derived token, keep its surface form and source alignment. If a compatibility-normalized feature is 50, record that it derives from the surface span ５０ rather than replacing the original text.






flowchart LR
    A[Immutable source] --> B[NFC display view]
    A --> C[NFKC matching view]
    B --> D[Surface tokens + offsets]
    C --> E[Search or numeric features]
    D --> F[Sentiment model]
    E --> F
    A --> G[Human audit]
    D --> G




Figure 10: One source can support multiple task-specific views without destroying evidence.





This architecture costs more than calling .lower() and deleting punctuation. It also makes errors explainable and future changes possible.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
11.1 Conceptual questions

Explain why the number of Python code points in a string may differ from the number of symbols a user perceives.
Give a task where lowercasing is helpful and another where it may remove signal.
Why can two valid tokenizers disagree without either being universally wrong?
Explain the difference between canonical and compatibility equivalence.
Why should a model prediction be stored with source offsets?

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
11.3 Tokenizer experiment
Implement the teaching regex tokenizer from this chapter and compare it with spaCy on at least twenty adversarial examples. Organize failures into categories such as contractions, URLs, numeric expressions, abbreviations, Arabic clitics, CJK text, and emoji. Propose two rule changes and add regression tests before implementing them.

title: Technical Reference: Text Processing
text:
11.4 Pipeline design
Design a preprocessing policy for one of these applications:

multilingual sentiment analysis;
exact legal-document search;
social-media named-entity recognition; or
duplicate product-title detection.

Document what you preserve, normalize, tokenize, and discard. For every destructive operation, explain why the lost distinction is irrelevant or acceptably risky for the chosen task.

title: Introduction to NLP
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Chapter 1 · Tasks, eras, and breakthroughs
Natural language processing sits at a remarkable intersection: human communication, computational models, and real-world decisions. This course is about understanding that intersection well enough to build useful systems—and to recognize where those systems succeed, fail, or mislead.
We begin with the map rather than the machinery. Today we will see what NLP systems do, compare three ways of building them, and trace the breakthroughs that produced modern language models. In the next chapter, we will slow down and ask how written language becomes something a model can process.

text:

1.2 Assessment at a glance
The intended balance keeps most of the grade on sustained, reproducible work.






pie showData
    title Assessment balance
    "Coding-project portfolio" : 45

Figure 2: Proposed assessment balance; final percentages will be confirmed on the logistics page.





The coding-project portfolio rewards consistent implementation and reflection. The final project asks you to formulate a problem, choose a defensible approach, evaluate it, and present the result. A short partial examination checks that you can connect the central ideas without relying on code.

title: Introduction to NLP
text:
2.1 One message, many possible tasks
Consider the message:

The battery lasts all day, but the camera struggles at night.

Different NLP systems could ask very different questions:



Task
Possible output




Sentiment analysis
Mixed


Aspect extraction
battery, camera


Aspect sentiment
Battery: positive; camera: negative


Summarization
Good battery, weak low-light camera


Translation
The same meaning in another language


Retrieval
Products with stronger night photography


Dialogue
A follow-up question about the user’s priorities



The text is identical, but the task determines what information matters. There is no universally correct representation of language independent of a goal.






flowchart LR
    X[One review] --> A{Task lens}
    A --> B[Label<br/>mixed sentiment]
    A --> C[Entities<br/>battery, camera]
    A --> D[Summary<br/>strength + weakness]
    A --> E[Response<br/>helpful recommendation]

    classDef input fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef lens fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef output fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a

    class A lens
    class B,C,D,E output




Figure 4: The task acts as a lens: the same language is transformed into different useful outputs.

title: Introduction to NLP
section: 3.1 Era I · Tell the machine the rules
text:
3.1 Era I · Tell the machine the rules
A rule-based system uses knowledge written explicitly by people:
beautiful  → +1
good       → +1
not good   → reverse the score
This approach is transparent and can work well in a narrow domain. Its weakness is coverage: every new expression, exception, and context may require another rule.

title: Introduction to NLP
section: 3.2 Era II · Learn patterns from examples
text:
3.2 Era II · Learn patterns from examples
A statistical classifier receives labeled reviews and estimates which observable features predict each label. Instead of assigning weights manually, it learns them from data.






flowchart LR
    A[Labeled text] --> B[Feature extraction<br/>counts, n-grams]
    B --> C[Learning algorithm]
    C --> D[Estimated weights]
    E[New text] --> F[Same feature extraction]
    D --> G[Classifier]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Prediction]

    classDef data fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef process fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef model fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A,E data
    class B,C,F process
    class D,G,H model




Figure 6: The classical statistical-learning recipe.





Statistical learning scales beyond hand-written rules, but its representation is often shallow. A bag of words knows that good occurred; it does not naturally understand why not good differs from good.

title: Introduction to NLP
section: 3.3 Era III · Learn representations and reuse knowledge
text:
3.3 Era III · Learn representations and reuse knowledge
Neural models learn both the representation and the prediction function. Modern Transformers go further: they first learn from enormous collections of text, then reuse that knowledge for a particular task.






flowchart LR
    A[Large text collections] --> B[Pretraining]
    B --> C[General language model]
    C --> D[Fine-tuning]
    C --> E[Prompting]
    C --> F[Retrieval augmentation]
    D --> G[Task system]
    E --> G
    F --> G

    classDef data fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef learn fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef model fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A data
    class B,D,E,F learn
    class C,G model




Figure 7: Modern NLP separates broad pretraining from task-specific adaptation or prompting.





The newer method is not automatically the best choice. A small rule system may be cheaper, easier to audit, and more reliable for a stable narrow task. The right question is not “Which era won?” but which assumptions and trade-offs fit the problem?









Question
Rules
Statistical learning
Pretrained Transformers




Where does knowledge come from?
Human experts
Labeled examples
Pretraining data + task data/instructions


Representation
Designed by hand
Usually engineered features
Learned contextual representations


Data requirement
Low

Large pretraining; adaptation can use less labeled data

text:
4.1 The recurring pattern






flowchart LR
    A[Write rules] -->|learn weights| B[Design features]
    B -->|learn representations| C[Design architectures]
    C -->|pretrain broadly| D[Adapt with data and instructions]
    D -->|connect external knowledge| E[Build language systems]

    A -. human specification decreases .-> E
    E -. data, compute, and evaluation increase .-> A

    classDef old fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef middle fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef modern fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A old
    class B,C middle
    class D,E modern




Figure 9: Breakthroughs repeatedly move work from explicit human design into learning, while increasing the importance of data and evaluation.






4.1.1 Statistical language models
Counting sequences of words made uncertainty measurable. A model could assign probabilities to sentences, rank alternatives, and generate text—although it struggled with rare phrases and long-range context.


4.1.2 Distributed representations
Word embeddings replaced isolated symbols with vectors learned from usage. Similar contexts produced nearby representations, giving systems a geometric notion of relatedness.


4.1.3 Neural sequence models
Recurrent networks processed text in order and learned features jointly with the task. They improved sequence modeling but remained difficult to train over long contexts.


4.1.4 Attention
Attention allowed a model to focus directly on relevant parts of an input instead of compressing everything into a single fixed-size state.


4.1.5 Transformers
Transformers made attention the central mechanism and enabled much more parallel training. Their scalability helped make broad pretraining practical (Vaswani et al. 2017).


4.1.6 Pretraining and instruction following
A pretrained model can reuse patterns learned from broad text collections. Fine-tuning, prompting, and instruction tuning turn that general model toward specific behaviors.


4.1.7 Retrieval and tools
Modern systems can search external collections, cite retrieved evidence, call software tools, and combine language with images or audio. The language model becomes one component in a larger system.






WarningCapability is not understanding, and fluency is not evidence



Modern models can produce convincing language while being wrong, biased, outdated, or unsupported. Throughout the course, evaluation and error analysis will matter as much as model architecture.

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: Attention can rearrange—but cannot detect the rearrangement
text:
Attention can rearrange—but cannot detect the rearrangement


  ORDER A ALICE THANKED BOB Alice performs the action   ORDER B BOB THANKED ALICE Bob performs the action    SELF-ATTENTION same token vectors · same pairwise comparisons     outputs follow order Aoutputs follow order B 



reorder inputs with \(P\)\(operatorname{Attn}(PX)=P,operatorname{Attn}(X)\)outputs are merely reordered


Attention sees which tokens are present and how they match—but it needs another signal to know where each token occurs.


Self-attention without positional information is permutation equivariant; the Transformer therefore injects position representations into its inputs (Stanford CS224N, Lecture 5).

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: Token embeddings need a position signal
text:
Token embeddings need a position signal

A token embedding tells us what the token is—not where it occurs.


\[
\boxed{\mathbf{z}_i=\mathbf{e}(\text{token}_i)+\mathbf{p}_i}
\]



TOKEN IDENTITY\(\mathbf e(\text{token}_i)\)same word → same lexical vector


+


POSITION\(\mathbf p_i\)different location → different position vector


→


TRANSFORMER INPUT\(\mathbf z_i\)content and order arrive together



The vectors have the same dimension, so addition preserves one vector per token and changes none of the attention machinery.


The Transformer adds positional encodings to input embeddings before the first layer [Vaswani et al., 2017; The Illustrated Transformer].

section: The same token now looks different in a different place

The same token now looks different in a different place

KEEP THE WORD FIXED · MOVE ITS POSITION \(\mathbf e_{\text{cats}}=[1.0,\ 0.0]\)

  &= \boxed{[1.1,0.0]}
\end{aligned}
\]


same identity≠different input



micechasecats

  &= \mathbf e_{\text{cats}}+\mathbf p_3\\
  &= [1.0,0.0]+[-0.1,0.1]\\
  &= \boxed{[0.9,0.1]}

We know how to inject position. But what information should the vectors \(\mathbf p_1,\mathbf p_2,\ldots\) contain?


Because position is added before projection, the queries, keys, and values can become sensitive to both token identity and location.

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: Encode position with waves at different frequencies
text:
Encode position with waves at different frequencies


FIXED SINUSOIDAL ENCODING
\[
\begin{aligned}
PE(pos,2k)
  &=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)\\[0.45em]
PE(pos,2k+1)
  &=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

pos selects the token location k selects a coordinate pair d is the embedding dimension




       FAST CHANGEMEDIUM CHANGESLOW CHANGE TOKEN POSITION →




Each position receives a distinctive pattern across dimensions; nearby positions have related patterns, while different frequencies expose distance at several scales.


OTHER POSITION STRATEGIESlearned absolute embeddingsrelative position representations or biasesrotary position embeddings (RoPE)linear attention biases (ALiBi)


The fixed sine–cosine construction is from Vaswani et al., 2017. Modern alternatives include learned, relative, rotary, and linear-bias approaches; here we focus on the classical sinusoidal formulation.

section: Position is solved—but attention still only mixes
text:
Position is solved—but attention still only mixes


 POSITION-AWAREZ  ATTENTION 1mix across positions  ATTENTION 2mix again  ?transform features




WHAT ATTENTION DOESMove and combine information between positions


WHAT IS STILL MISSINGA position-wise nonlinear transformation of features



What small neural network can transform every token independently between attention layers?


Self-attention supplies weighted mixtures but no elementwise nonlinearity; the Transformer follows it with a position-wise feed-forward network (Stanford CS224N, Lecture 5).

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: Attention communicates; it does not deeply process each message
text:
Attention communicates; it does not deeply process each message

ATTENTION
Who should communicate with whom?


FEED-FORWARD NETWORK
How should the retrieved features be transformed?



Self-attention routes and combines information across positions; the following feed-forward network independently processes each resulting position (Stanford CS224N, Lecture 5).

section: The feed-forward network is a familiar two-layer MLP
text:
The feed-forward network is a familiar two-layer MLP

\[
\operatorname{FFN}(x)=W_2\,\operatorname{ReLU}(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
\]


The Transformer applies this same two-layer MLP independently to every token position; the original formulation uses ReLU [Vaswani et al., 2017].

text:
Unfold one Transformer stack


THE MAIN IDEA

MHA communicates: each token retrieves information from other positions.
FFN transforms: the same small MLP processes every token independently.
The two operations alternate throughout the stack.
Every layer keeps the sequence length and model width unchanged.


One block learns one round of communication followed by one round of feature transformation.

The computation is clear—but what prevents information from degrading as this stack becomes deep?


Attention and the position-wise FFN are the two computational sublayers repeated through the Transformer; residual connections and normalization make that repetition trainable.

The triangular mask lets every position train in parallel—without revealing the answer it is supposed to predict.


Decoder self-attention masks all connections to subsequent positions, preserving the autoregressive constraint (Vaswani et al., 2017).

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
Implement masking before the softmax


1 · COMPUTE SCORES
\[S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\]
One score for every query–key pair.


2 · ADD THE MASK
\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0 & j\le i\\
-\infty & j>i
\end{cases}
\]
Future scores become \(-\infty\).


3 · NORMALIZE
\[A=\operatorname{softmax}(S+M)\]
Because \(e^{-\infty}=0\), blocked positions receive exactly zero attention.



scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k)
scores = scores.masked_fill(causal_mask == 0, float("-inf"))
attention = softmax(scores, dim=-1)
output = attention @ V


Implementation check: apply the mask to the scores—not to the probabilities—and do it before softmax.


The mask is added to scaled dot-product scores before normalization; practical implementations commonly use an upper-triangular boolean mask with masked logits filled by \(-\infty\).

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: The ingredients work—but depth still needs a safe route
text:
The ingredients work—but depth still needs a safe route


OUR SELF-ATTENTION BUILDING BLOCK

Self-attention moves information between token positions.
Position representations tell an otherwise unordered operation where tokens occur.
Nonlinearities enter through the position-wise feed-forward network.
Masking prevents future information from leaking into a prediction.


One more requirement for depth: preserve a direct path for both information and gradients.
\[x \longrightarrow x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\]

The four necessities summarize slide 53 of Stanford CS224N, Lecture 5; residual connections add a direct identity path around each sublayer.

THE IDENTITY PATH
\[x^{(\ell)}=x^{(\ell-1)}+F(x^{(\ell-1)})\]

The sublayer learns only the correction \(F(x)\).
If that correction is not yet useful, the block can remain close to the identity function.
During backpropagation, the skip contributes a direct derivative of 1.


\[\frac{\partial x^{(\ell)}}{\partial x^{(\ell-1)}}=I+\frac{\partial F}{\partial x^{(\ell-1)}}\]

section: LayerNorm controls each token’s feature scale
text:
LayerNorm controls each token’s feature scale


ONE TOKEN · \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
\[\mu=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j\]
\[\sigma^2=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-\mu)^2\]
\[\widehat{x}_j=\frac{x_j-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}\]

\[y_j=\gamma_j\widehat{x}_j+\beta_j\]
\(\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) are learned.


Statistics are computed across the feature axis of each token independently.




 ACTIVATION TENSOR Xshape: B × T × d   one token vector x[b,t,:] FEATURES · dTOKENS · TBATCH · B reduce over d ONE PAIR PER TOKENμσ²μσ²μσ²μσ²each has shape B × T × 1 B and T stay separateonly d is collapsed

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
LayerNorm makes feature scale comparable


1 · MEAN\[\mu=\frac{1+2+3}{3}=2\]


2 · VARIANCE\[\sigma^2=\frac{(1-2)^2+(2-2)^2+(3-2)^2}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\]


3 · NORMALIZE\[\operatorname{LN}(x)=\frac{[1,2,3]-2}{\sqrt{2/3}}\approx[-1.22,\;0,\;1.22]\]




BEFORE
\([1,\;2,\;3]\)


AFTER
\([-1.22,\;0,\;1.22]\)


mean \(\approx 0\)variance \(\approx 1\)



The learned vectors \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) can then rescale and shift each feature; normalization does not force every layer to remain standardized.


Layer normalization computes statistics within each token representation and then applies learned elementwise gain and bias (Ba et al., 2016).

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: LayerNorm in PyTorch: explicit and predefined
text:
LayerNorm in PyTorch: explicit and predefined


FROM THE EQUATIONS
import torch
from torch import nn

def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    var = x.var(
        dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False
    )
    x_hat = (x - mean) * torch.rsqrt(var + eps)
    return gamma * x_hat + beta

gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d_model))
beta  = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_model))
y = layer_norm(x, gamma, beta)


THE nn MODULE
import torch
from torch import nn

# x.shape == (batch, tokens, d_model)
norm = nn.LayerNorm(
    normalized_shape=d_model,
    eps=1e-5,
    elementwise_affine=True,
)

y = norm(x)

assert y.shape == x.shape

normalized_shape=d_model normalizes the last axis, then learns one γ and β per feature.




\(X: B\times T\times d\)normalize dim=-1\(Y: B\times T\times d\)


PyTorch nn.LayerNorm(d_model) normalizes over the final dimension, uses the biased variance estimator (unbiased=False), and applies learnable elementwise affine parameters by default. PyTorch LayerNorm documentation.

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: The classical Transformer wraps each sublayer with Add & Norm
text:
The classical Transformer wraps each sublayer with Add & Norm


POST-NORM · ORIGINAL TRANSFORMER

A residual path carries \(x\) around the sublayer.
The two paths are added.
LayerNorm stabilizes the combined representation.
The pattern is applied after both MHA and the FFN.


\[\operatorname{LayerNorm}\!\left(x+\operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\right)\]




 INPUT x  MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION   ADD & NORM  FEED-FORWARD NETWORK   ADD & NORM




Residuals preserve a route through depth; LayerNorm controls the representation carried along that route.


The original Transformer uses post-norm residual sublayers, commonly summarized as “Add & Norm” (Vaswani et al., 2017).

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: A Transformer decoder repeats one complete block
text:
A Transformer decoder repeats one complete block


THE COMPLETE DECODER

A Transformer decoder is a stack of \(L\) decoder blocks.
Every block contains:

masked multi-head self-attention,
residual connection + LayerNorm,
position-wise FFN,
residual connection + LayerNorm.

The same architecture repeats, but each layer has its own learned parameters.
Linear projection and softmax convert the final state into next-token probabilities.


\[Z^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{DecoderBlock}_{\ell}(Z^{(\ell-1)})\]




 LINEAR + SOFTMAXNEXT-TOKEN PROBABILITIES   DECODER BLOCKℓ = 1, …, L   MASKED MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION  ADD & NORM  POSITION-WISE FFN  ADD & NORM     SHIFTED TARGET EMBEDDINGS+ POSITION




The decoder-stack summary follows the original Transformer and the component list in Stanford CS224N, Lecture 5, slide 64. Cross-attention is added later for an encoder–decoder model.

THE ENCODER STACK

A Transformer encoder is a stack of \(L\) encoder blocks.
Every block contains:

RNN’s repair
Carry an evolving state beyond a fixed suffix.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: Build the neural language model from that example
text:
Build the neural language model from that example





Original Figure 1 from Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent, and Christian Jauvin (2003), “A Neural Probabilistic Language Model,” Journal of Machine Learning Research 3: 1137–1155, p. 1142. Paper and PDF.


This is Bengio et al.’s window-based neural probabilistic language model, shown with the same concrete context from the previous slide.

Begin at the left: each discrete word index selects a learned vector from a shared embedding table.
Concatenate the vectors for the fixed context window into one vector, \(\mathbf x=(C(w_{t-1}),C(w_{t-2}),\ldots,C(w_{t-n+1}))\).
The hidden layer learns distributed features of that context: \(\mathbf a=\tanh(\mathbf d+H\mathbf x)\).
The output layer produces one unnormalized log-probability per vocabulary item: \(\mathbf y=\mathbf b+W\mathbf x+U\mathbf a\); softmax normalizes these scores.
In the original paper, the embedding parameters and probability network are learned jointly by maximizing the training-corpus log likelihood.
The curved dashed route is the paper’s optional direct connection \(W\mathbf x\). When direct connections are disabled, \(W=0\).
Emphasize the limitation without developing it yet: this is still a fixed context window. We will decide in the next review how to use that boundary to motivate recurrence.

We need one neural architecture that can process any-length input without enlarging its parameter matrices.


Adapted from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” Stanford CS224N/Ling284, Winter 2026, slide 24. Lecture slides.



Begin with the two improvements over an n-gram model: learned representations remove the exact-count sparsity problem, and the model does not store a table of observed n-grams.
Reveal problem 1: the four-word window discards “proctor,” even if that word is useful for predicting “exams.”
Reveal problem 2 and the lower expanded vector together. If the context contains \(k\) embeddings of dimension \(d_e\), the concatenated vector has dimension \(kd_e\). Therefore \(W\) has shape \(d_h\times kd_e\) and gains \(d_h d_e\) parameters for every new position.
Reveal problem 3: choosing a larger \(k\) delays the boundary but never removes it.
Reveal problem 4: concatenation assigns a separate block of \(W\) to each position. The same word is processed differently in position 1 and position 2; the architecture has no symmetry across time.
Final reveal: ask for an architecture whose parameter count is independent of sequence length and whose same transformation can be reused at every position. This is the opening for recurrence; do not show the RNN equation yet.

Read the diagram before the equations. The current input \(\mathbf x_t\) and previous state \(\mathbf h_{t-1}\) meet inside one recurrent cell.

Forward computation → · gradient flow ←




1 · OUTPUT ERROR
\[
\boldsymbol\delta_z=\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t
\]


2 · REACH THE HIDDEN STATE
\[
\mathbf g_h=U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z
\]


3 · PASS THROUGH TANH
\[

\]


4 · FOLLOW BOTH INPUT BRANCHES
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{W_h}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a\mathbf h_{t-1}^{\top},
&\nabla_{\mathbf h_{t-1}}L_t&=W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a\\
\nabla_{W_x}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a\mathbf x_t^{\top},
&\nabla_{\mathbf b_h}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a
\end{aligned}
\]




Local RNN backpropagation follows the computational graph from softmax cross-entropy through the hidden-state update (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, Ch. 9).



Keep the complete forward cell visible, but reveal the backward path one stage at a time. Each numbered gradient overlay on the left is synchronized with the formula carrying the same number on the right.
Stage 1: for softmax with cross-entropy, the derivative with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the one-hot target, \(\boldsymbol\delta_z=\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t\).
Stage 2: multiply by \(U^\top\) to move the error from output space into hidden-state space. For this first local derivation, \(\mathbf g_h\) contains only the contribution from the output at time \(t\).
Stage 3: differentiate the tanh nonlinearity elementwise. Keep \(\boldsymbol\delta_a\) visible; it is the reusable error signal for every branch entering the cell pre-activation.
Stage 4: the same \(\boldsymbol\delta_a\) produces gradients for \(W_h\), \(W_x\), and \(\mathbf b_h\). The branch \(W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a\) sends credit to the previous hidden state.
End by pointing to \(\nabla_{\mathbf h_{t-1}}L_t\). We have derived one local backward step; the next slide expands the objective from one output loss to all output losses in the sequence.

Token-level cross-entropy losses and their sum over a sequence follow the recurrent language-model objective (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, Ch. 9).



Keep the concrete prediction visible: after “the students opened their,” the target is “books,” and the model assigns it probability \(0.62\).

Reveal the total sequence objective as the sum of those losses.

BACKPROPAGATION RULE AT A BRANCH
\[

\]
Every downstream route contributes; the contributions add.




Gradient accumulation at a branching node is the multivariable chain rule applied to the unfolded recurrent computation graph (Goodfellow et al. 2016, Chs. 6 and 10; Jurafsky and Martin 2026, Ch. 9).



This slide is the worked answer to the preceding PAUSE question at the level of one hidden state.
Read the forward graph first. The state \(\mathbf h_t\) has two downstream uses: it produces the current output and it enters the next recurrent state.
Reveal the blue path from \(J^{(t)}\). It contributes \(U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z^{(t)}\).
Reveal the path returning from \(\mathbf h_{t+1}\). It contributes \(W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a^{(t+1)}\).
Reveal the plus sign and total gradient. Backpropagation does not choose one route; it sums all downstream contributions at the shared node.
This same principle will repeat at every hidden state when the RNN is unfolded through time.
