Backpropagation through time is ordinary backpropagation applied to the RNN unfolded as a computation graph (Werbos 1990; Goodfellow et al. 2016, Ch. 10; Jurafsky and Martin 2026, Ch. 9).



This slide is intentionally illustration-only. Let the spatial structure carry the explanation.
First read the solid teal forward pass: each input updates a hidden state; every hidden state produces a token-level loss; \(W_h\) is reused along the horizontal chain.
Reveal the first translucent-blue layer: every loss sends a local gradient into its hidden state.
Reveal the second layer: those gradients then travel backward through the recurrent chain, from later states toward earlier states.
Reveal the curved paths into the parameter hub: because the same \(W_h\), \(W_x\), and \(U\) were used repeatedly, every time step contributes to the gradients of the same parameter tensors.
Final reveal: the curved paths collect every time-step contribution into the shared parameter gradient; sum them, then perform one optimizer update.
End with the full backward chain visible. The unresolved question is now how repeated Jacobian products behave when credit must travel across many time steps.

The problem is not “recurrence” alone. It is the product of many local transformations: repeated contraction forgets; repeated expansion destabilizes.


Vanishing and exploding gradients in recurrent networks are analyzed through products of Jacobians and their spectral behavior (Bengio et al. 1994; Pascanu et al. 2013).



Return to the two scalar cases from the PAUSE slide.
Read the upper chain from right to left: \(1\), \(0.6\), \(0.36\), \(0.216\), \(0.1296\). The translucent arrows deliberately fade with the gradient.
Read the lower chain: \(1\), \(1.5\), \(2.25\), \(3.375\), \(5.0625\). The orange arrows become more opaque and thicker as the signal grows.
Reveal the consequences. A vanishing gradient prevents distant evidence from teaching early recurrent states. An exploding gradient produces unstable parameter updates and can create numerical overflow.
Reveal the synthesis last. The scalar example is an intuition pump; in the vector RNN, matrix Jacobians contract or expand different directions at different rates.
End with a forward-looking question for the next review: can the architecture create a path along which useful information and gradients travel with less repeated distortion?

Apply the optimizer updateUse g̃ instead of the unstable g.





ALGORITHM · CLIP BY GLOBAL NORM

input: gradient g, threshold τ

r ← ‖g‖₂

if r > τ:
    g̃ ← (τ / r) g
else:
    g̃ ← g

θ ← θ − η g̃


g̃ = min(1, τ / ‖g‖₂) g

Norm capped at τ; direction preserved.





WHAT CLIPPING FIXES
Exploding gradients
Prevents one enormous update from destabilizing training.


WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX
Vanishing gradients
It cannot restore distant credit that has already faded.


Can the recurrent cell create a protected memory path instead of repeatedly rewriting everything?



Global-norm clipping is a practical treatment for exploding gradients, but it does not solve long-term credit assignment (Pascanu et al. 2013; Goodfellow et al. 2016, Ch. 10).



Reveal the slide as a practical intervention, not as a new recurrent architecture.
Stage 1: after BPTT has accumulated the complete gradient, compute its global Euclidean norm. In the visible example, the norm is \(18\), above the threshold \(\tau=5\).
Stage 2: multiply the whole gradient vector by \(5/18\). The new norm is exactly \(5\), but every component is scaled by the same positive factor, so the update direction is preserved.
Match the visual shortening on the left to the formula and pseudocode on the right.
Stage 3: pass the clipped gradient to the optimizer. Clipping changes the step magnitude only when the norm exceeds the threshold.
Reveal the final comparison. Clipping is highly useful for explosions, but it does not make a tiny long-range gradient large again.
End on the question about a protected memory path. This creates the need for gated recurrent cells without introducing their equations yet.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: Two gated answers to fragile memory
text:
Two gated answers to fragile memory

GATED-RNN HEYDAY · roughly 2012–2018LSTM: 1997 · GRU: 2014 · Transformer: 2017, followed by a gradual transition away from recurrence




LSTMseparate cell state · three gate roles


 cₜ₋₁cₜ ×+ forget input write out  [hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ]hₜ


RETAIN · WRITE · EXPOSEA distinct memory highway cₜ crosses time.




GRUone hidden state · two gates


 hₜ₋₁hₜ +× reset r update z candidate  [hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ]


RESET · INTERPOLATEThe old state and a candidate share one highway hₜ.




LSTM introduced an explicit memory path (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997); GRU introduced a simpler gated state update (Cho et al. 2014). The Transformer appeared in 2017 (Vaswani et al. 2017).



“2012–2018” is a useful label for the gated-RNN heyday, not the invention period. LSTM dates to 1997 and GRU to 2014.
The Transformer arrived in 2017; the transition was gradual and task-dependent, not an overnight replacement.
Keep this overview at the flow level only. LSTM separates memory c from the visible hidden state h. GRU combines them into one state.
These are clean redraws of the classical mechanisms so students will recognize the standard paper diagrams later.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
LSTM: protect, write, then expose



 cₜ₋₁cₜ ×+ ×× σ · fₜ σ · iₜ tanh · gₜ σ · oₜ  [hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ]hₜ   




1 · RETAIN OR FORGETforget gate

fₜ = σ(W_f [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_f)



2 · PREPARE A WRITEinput gate + candidate

iₜ = σ(W_i [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_i)


gₜ = tanh(W_g [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_g)



3 · UPDATE MEMORY

cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ gₜ



4 · EXPOSE PART OF IToutput gate

oₜ = σ(W_o [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_o)


hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ)



KEY PATHcₜ uses an additive update that can preserve memory and gradient flow.




Pedagogical redraw of the LSTM gated memory mechanism (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; Goodfellow et al. 2016, Ch. 10).



Reveal the forget path, then the write path, then the exposed hidden state. Match each colored overlay to the equation card with the same reveal.
Keep the discussion shallow; the coding project will handle dimensions and implementation.
The main conceptual difference is the additive cell-state update. LSTM does not guarantee perfect memory, but it creates a less distorted route.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
GRU: reset, propose, then interpolate



 hₜ₋₁hₜ +× σ · rₜ tanh · h̃ₜ σ · zₜ  [hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ]   




1 · RESET THE OLD STATEreset gate

rₜ = σ(W_r [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_r)



2 · PROPOSE A CANDIDATE

h̃ₜ = tanh(W_h [rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_h)



3 · INTERPOLATEupdate gate

zₜ = σ(W_z [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_z)


hₜ = (1 − zₜ) ⊙ hₜ₋₁ + zₜ ⊙ h̃ₜ



KEY PATHzₜ directly mixes the old state with the proposed new state.




GRU formulation introduced with the RNN Encoder–Decoder (Cho et al. 2014) and compared empirically with LSTM (Chung et al. 2014).



Reveal reset, candidate, then interpolation. Match the highlighted arrow to the equation card.
GRU combines memory and visible hidden state into one vector, with fewer gate roles than LSTM.
End on the direct mixture between old and candidate state. Leave implementation details for the coding project.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: From language modeling to neural machine translation
text:
From language modeling to neural machine translation

MT · MACHINE TRANSLATIONGenerate a sentence in a target language that preserves the meaning of a source sentence.





SOURCE · FRENCHLe colis arrivera demain.


one sequence→another sequence


TARGET · ENGLISHThe package will arrive tomorrow.


Learn p(target sentence | source sentence)



2016 · A PRODUCTION TURNING POINT Google Neural Machine Translation One end-to-end neural system replaced the previous phrase-based translation pipeline. The task was no longer a research demo—it was operating at global scale.




TRANSLATION BECAME EVERYDAY INFRASTRUCTURE



MESSAGEScross-language conversations


WEB + SEARCHaccess beyond one language


MEETINGScaptions and live interpretation


TRAVEL + SUPPORTcommunication at the point of need



Different interfaces—one recurring need: communicate across languages.




The task is simple to state—but difficult to model: how can a system preserve an entire source sentence while generating a new one?


Google described its large-scale Neural Machine Translation system in 2016 (Wu et al. 2016). This sequence-to-sequence problem later became the original proving ground for the Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017).



Begin with the acronym: MT means Machine Translation. Define the task before introducing any architecture.
Reveal the concrete French–English pair. The output is not a word-for-word substitution: it must preserve meaning and produce a fluent target sentence.
Reveal the headline, then one modern use at a time. Do not read all four uses as a list; let each new setting broaden the same task.
When the 2016 milestone appears, it covers and retires the example. This is not the invention of NMT: it marks Google’s highly visible production-scale deployment of GNMT.
Reveal the final question last. It creates the need for the encoder–decoder architecture on the next slide.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: One recurrent chain: read, then write
text:
One recurrent chain: read, then write

The encoder’s final hidden state becomes the decoder’s initial hidden state.



     1 · ENCODE THE SOURCE Read every French token into a running state.  h₁ h₂ h₃ h₄ Le colis arrivera demain SOURCE SEQUENCE · x₁ … x₄     c CONTEXT c = h₄ all source information    2 · DECODE THE TARGET Start from c, then generate one English token at a time.  s₁ s₂ s₃ s₄ The package will arrive tomorrow TARGET SEQUENCE · y₁ … y₄ 



The whole source sentence must pass through one fixed-size vector, c.


The sequence-to-sequence encoder–decoder maps a variable-length source to a variable-length target through a fixed-dimensional state (Sutskever et al. 2014; Cho et al. 2014).



Reveal only the blue encoder region first. Follow the French tokens and point out that its state is updated after every input.
Reveal the bridge second. The final encoder state h4 is renamed context c and used to initialize the decoder.
Reveal the coral decoder region third. It continues recurrent computation, but now produces the English sequence token by token.
“One RNN reads; another writes” describes two recurrent roles. The visual is one continuous recurrent chain joined by c; implementations may use separate encoder and decoder parameters.
Reveal the fixed-size-vector statement last. This is the limitation that will make attention necessary.

ONE NAME FOR THE PATTERNConditional language model


P(y | x) = ∏t=1T P(yt | y<t, x)


LANGUAGE MODELgenerates y token by tokenCONDITIONALevery prediction also depends on x



Representative early encoder–decoder applications include summarization, dialogue, linearized parsing, and code generation (Rush et al. 2015; Vinyals and Le 2015; Vinyals et al. 2015; Yin and Neubig 2017).



Start from the abstract pattern. Translation used source language x and target language y, but the architecture only requires an input and a generated output.
Reveal one task card at a time; each replaces the previous card so students inspect one mapping rather than scan four boxes.
For parsing, state the qualification explicitly: parsing becomes conditional sequence generation when the tree is linearized into tokens. Not every parser is a language model.
After code generation, replace the example with four compact mappings. The changing task is defined by what x and y mean.
Reveal the name and factorization with the synthesis. It is a language model because y is generated autoregressively. It is conditional because x remains an argument of every next-token distribution.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: Training seq2seq: loss there, credit everywhere
text:
Training seq2seq: loss there, credit everywhere

The targets supervise the decoder outputs—then backpropagation trains the entire encoder–decoder chain.



  ENCODER · NO DIRECT TARGET LOSSDECODER · PREDICT TARGET TOKENS h₁h₂h₃h₄c s₁s₂s₃s₄ Lecolisarriverademainŷ₁ŷ₂ŷ₃ŷ₄  J⁽¹⁾J⁽²⁾J⁽³⁾J⁽⁴⁾J⁽ᵗ⁾ = −log p(yₜ | y<t, x) J = J⁽¹⁾ + J⁽²⁾ + J⁽³⁾ + J⁽⁴⁾ ∂J flows through decoder → c → encoder




WHERE IS LOSS COMPUTED?Only where target tokens are predicted.


WHAT GETS UPDATED?Decoder parameters, context path, and encoder parameters.



Sequence-to-sequence models are trained end-to-end with target-side token losses and gradients propagated through the full computation graph (Sutskever et al. 2014; Goodfellow et al. 2016, Ch. 10).



Reveal the forward computation first. The encoder reads source tokens; the context initializes the decoder; the decoder predicts target tokens.
Reveal the four decoder losses. Each prediction is compared with its gold target token using cross-entropy. No separate loss is attached to the encoder states.
Sum the token losses into one sequence objective.
Reveal the translucent backward path. Although supervision appears on the decoder side, the chain rule carries credit through every decoder state, through c, and back into every encoder state.
End with the two-answer synthesis: loss location and parameter-update reach are different questions.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
One vector must remember everything


 ENCODER · READ THE WHOLE SOURCEDECODER · GENERATE THE WHOLE TARGET h₁h₂h₃h₄cONE FIXED-SIZE VECTOR s₁s₂s₃s₄ LecolisarriverademainThepackagewill arrivetomorrow every source detail must survive inside c



PAUSE · FIND THE LIMITATION What happens when the source is long, information-rich, or difficult to compress into one vector?



THE BOTTLENECKThe decoder can consult only c—even when it needs one specific source detail.


COMING NEXT WEEKATTENTIONCan the decoder recover what it needs without forcing everything through one fixed-size memory?



The fixed-length context vector was a central limitation of early encoder–decoder translation models; attention was introduced to address it (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

Reveal the translucent compression curves and pause. Ask what information the decoder can access after the encoder has finished.
Let students name the fixed-context bottleneck before revealing the answer.

A tiny regex tokenizer
import re

pattern = r"\b\w+(?:['’]\w+)?\b|[^\w\s]"

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Recall: one RNN reads, another writes
text:
Recall: one RNN reads, another writes

The encoder’s final hidden state becomes the decoder’s initial hidden state.



  1 · ENCODE THE SOURCERead every French token into a running state. h₁h₂h₃h₄ LecolisarriverademainSOURCE SEQUENCE · x₁ … x₄  cCONTEXTc = h₄all source information  2 · DECODE THE TARGETStart from c, then generate one English token at a time. s₁s₂s₃s₄ Thepackagewill arrivetomorrowTARGET SEQUENCE · y₁ … y₄ 



The whole source sentence reaches the decoder through one fixed-size vector, c.


This is the recurrent encoder–decoder architecture developed in the previous lecture (Sutskever et al. 2014; Cho et al. 2014).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
One vector must remember everything


 ENCODER · READ THE WHOLE SOURCEDECODER · GENERATE THE WHOLE TARGET h₁h₂h₃h₄cONE FIXED-SIZE VECTOR s₁s₂s₃s₄ LecolisarriverademainThepackagewill arrivetomorrow every source detail must survive inside c



PAUSE · FIND THE LIMITATION When the decoder needs “demain,” what source representation can it inspect directly?


Early recurrent seq2seq models summarize a variable-length source with a fixed-dimensional context (Cho et al. 2014).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: The bottleneck is not only storage—it is access
text:
The bottleneck is not only storage—it is access


THE ONLY AVAILABLE PATH

 Le colis arrivera demain  c  s₄ → “tomorrow”

\[p(y_t\mid y_{<t},\,\mathbf{c})\]



1 · COMPRESSEvery source detail competes for space inside the same vector.


2 · CARRYEarly information must survive every later encoder update.


3 · RECOVEREvery decoder step must reconstruct what it needs from c alone.




The decoder does not lack the source sentence—it lacks a direct way to retrieve the relevant part.


What if each decoder step could look back at all encoder states and choose where to focus?


Attention was introduced to replace the single fixed-context dependency with learned access to encoder states (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Keep every source memory

Instead of asking the decoder to recover everything from \(c=h_4\), preserve all encoder states.



  BEFORE · ONE SUMMARY h₁h₂h₃h₄ Lecolisarriverademain  c s₄   NOW · A SET OF MEMORIES h₁h₂h₃h₄ Lecolisarriverademain  s₄needs “tomorrow” 



The decoder gains direct paths to earlier source representations—but it still needs a rule for choosing among them.


Attention lets each decoder step use the sequence of encoder states rather than only the encoder’s final state (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Think of attention as a soft lookup
text:
Think of attention as a soft lookup


DECODER’S REQUEST
“Which source memory helps me generate tomorrow?”

current decoder state \(s_4\)




Le\(h_1\)weak match


colis\(h_2\)weak match


arrivera\(h_3\)some match


demain\(h_4\)strong match





HARD LOOKUPChoose one entry\(h_4\) only


SOFT LOOKUPBlend every entrymostly \(h_4\), a little of the others



At its core, attention is learned weighted averaging: a request is compared with stored representations, then the retrieved values are blended Stanford CS224N Lecture 5.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Turn compatibility scores into weights


GIVEN · DECODER STEP 4 We need to generate “tomorrow.” The model assigns one compatibility score to each source memory:



Le\(e_{4,1}=0.0\)


colis\(e_{4,2}=0.0\)


arrivera\(e_{4,3}=0.7\)


demain\(e_{4,4}=1.8\)




PAUSE · NORMALIZE THE SCORES
Apply softmax. What four attention weights do you expect—and what must they add up to?
\[
\alpha_{4,i}=\frac{\exp(e_{4,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{4}\exp(e_{4,j})}
\]


Additive attention normalizes alignment scores into a probability distribution over source positions (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Softmax creates an attention distribution


EXPONENTIATE\([e^0,\ e^0,\ e^{0.7},\ e^{1.8}]\)\(\approx[1.00,\ 1.00,\ 2.01,\ 6.05]\)


NORMALIZEdivide by \(10.06\)\(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_4\approx[0.10,\ 0.10,\ 0.20,\ 0.60]\)




Le0.10


colis0.10


arrivera0.20


demain0.60



\(\alpha_{4,i}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_{4,i}=1\)  →  the weights form a distribution over source positions.


Softmax preserves relative compatibility while turning arbitrary scores into nonnegative weights that sum to one Stanford CS224N Lecture 5.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Retrieve a weighted context

For visibility, suppose each encoder memory has only two coordinates:



Le\(h_1=[1,0]\)\(\alpha_{4,1}=0.10\)


colis\(h_2=[0,1]\)\(\alpha_{4,2}=0.10\)


arrivera\(h_3=[1,1]\)\(\alpha_{4,3}=0.20\)


demain\(h_4=[0,2]\)\(\alpha_{4,4}=0.60\)



\[
\begin{aligned}
c_4 &= \sum_{i=1}^{4}\alpha_{4,i}h_i\\
&=0.10[1,0]+0.10[0,1]+0.20[1,1]+0.60[0,2]\\
&=\boxed{[0.30,\ 1.50]}
\end{aligned}
\]


Because “demain” receives the largest weight, its representation contributes most strongly—but the lookup remains soft and differentiable.


The attention context is the weighted sum of encoder states; the decoder uses a different context \(c_t\) at each target step (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Attention repeats three operations


1SCOREHow compatible is the current request with each memory?\(e_{t,i}\)


→


2NORMALIZETurn all scores into a distribution.\(\alpha_{t,i}=\operatorname{softmax}(e_{t,i})\)


→


3RETRIEVEBlend memories using those weights.\(c_t=\sum_i\alpha_{t,i}h_i\)



One decoder step receives one task-dependent view of the source—not one universal sentence summary.


The mechanism is clear—but how does the model learn and compute the compatibility score \(e_{t,i}\)?


This score–normalize–retrieve abstraction is the common structure behind recurrent attention and later dot-product attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al. 2015; Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Give the request and memories distinct roles
text:
Give the request and memories distinct roles

At decoder step 4, the model must match what it needs now against what each source position offers.



  SOURCE MEMORY BANK Leh₁ colish₂ arriverah₃ demainh₄   k₁k₂k₃k₄ KEYS · describe what each memory can match   generate “tomorrow”s₄q₄QUERY · describes the current need  compare q₄ with every key → one score per source position



The decoder supplies the query; the encoder supplies the keys and values. Information crosses from source to target—hence cross-attention.


Cross-attention uses a target-side query with source-side keys and values Vaswani et al. (2017); Stanford CS224N Lecture 5.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: One source state performs two jobs
text:
One source state performs two jobs


ENCODER STATE

demain


\(h_4\)




MATCHING ADDRESS\(k_4=W_Kh_4\)Compared with the query“Is this memory relevant?”


RETRIEVABLE CONTENT\(v_4=W_Vh_4\)Added to the context if relevant“What information should I return?”




A key is used to decide the weight. A value is multiplied by that weight. They come from the same state, but they do different work.


The key–value terminology makes explicit the separation between addressing a memory and retrieving its content Vaswani et al. (2017); Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Compute compatibility with a dot product
text:
Compute compatibility with a dot product


QUERY\(q_4=[1,1]\)what the decoder needs



Le\(k_1=[0,0]\)


colis\(k_2=[0,0]\)


arrivera\(k_3=[0.4,0.3]\)


demain\(k_4=[1.0,0.8]\)




PAUSE · CALCULATE FOUR SCORES
Compute \(e_{4,i}=q_4^\top k_i\). Which source key best matches the decoder’s request?


Dot-product attention measures query–key compatibility using an inner product (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: The query selects a matching key
text:
The query selects a matching key


Le\([1,1]^\top[0,0]\)\(e_{4,1}=0.0\)


colis\([1,1]^\top[0,0]\)\(e_{4,2}=0.0\)


arrivera\([1,1]^\top[0.4,0.3]\)\(e_{4,3}=0.7\)


demain\([1,1]^\top[1.0,0.8]\)\(e_{4,4}=1.8\)



\[
[0.0,0.0,0.7,1.8]\xrightarrow{\text{softmax}}[0.10,0.10,0.20,0.60]
\]


The large dot product does not retrieve \(k_4\). It only gives the position a large retrieval weight.


The dot products become logits; softmax converts them into attention weights (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Use the weights to retrieve values
text:
Use the weights to retrieve values


 QUERYq₄ MATCH KEYSk₁k₂k₃k₄ 0.100.100.200.60 WEIGHT VALUESv₁v₂v₃v₄  CONTEXTc₄DECODERs₄ c₄ = 0.10v₁ + 0.10v₂ + 0.20v₃ + 0.60v₄



Match against keys; retrieve from values. The highest-weight value contributes most to \(c_4\).


Attention output is a weighted sum of values, with weights determined by query–key compatibility (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: A new query creates a new alignment
text:
A new query creates a new alignment



αₜ,ᵢ


Le

NEW DECODER STATE\(s_t\rightarrow q_t\)


NEW SCORE ROW\(e_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i\)


NEW SOURCE VIEW\(c_t=\sum_i\alpha_{t,i}v_i\)




Cross-attention is a learned, differentiable alignment: each target step asks a different question of the same source memory bank.


What changes if the queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence?


Attention weights can be visualized as soft source–target alignments, though they should not automatically be treated as complete explanations (Bahdanau et al. 2015).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Keep the mechanism—change where the roles come from
text:
Keep the mechanism—change where the roles come from


CROSS-ATTENTION

target state→ querysource states→ keys + values

Two different sequences


SELF-ATTENTION

sequence states→ queriesthe same states→ keys + values

One sequence plays all three roles




QUERY · POSITION \(i\)\(q_i=W_Qx_i\)what token \(i\) is looking for


KEY · POSITION \(j\)\(k_j=W_Kx_j\)what token \(j\) can match


VALUE · POSITION \(j\)\(v_j=W_Vx_j\)what token \(j\) can return



Token \(i\) asks a question about the sequence; every token \(j\) offers a key to match and a value to retrieve.


Self-attention draws queries, keys, and values from the same sequence Vaswani et al. (2017); Stanford CS224N Lecture 5.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Which earlier token explains “it”?

Theanimalwastiredbecauseitran


To represent “it”, the model should combine the token itself with the context that identifies its referent.


PAUSE · CHOOSE THE USEFUL CONTEXT
If “it” sends one query to every token, which token should receive the largest attention weight? What information should come back?


Pronoun resolution is a standard intuition for contextual token representations in illustrated explanations of self-attention Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer.

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: One token performs a soft lookup
text:
One token performs a soft lookup


  Theanimalwastiredbecauseitran  KEYSk₁k₂k₃k₄k₅k₆k₇ q₆QUERY FROM “it” 0.550.15 contextual “it” = mostly animal + it



The output at position 6 is no longer a representation of “it” alone—it is “it” interpreted in this sentence.


Self-attention forms a contextual representation by taking a query-dependent weighted sum of values from the same sequence (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Every token asks its own question
text:
Every token asks its own question


 INPUTSOUTPUTS Theanimalwastiredbecauseitran   z₁z₂z₃z₄z₅z₆z₇ all seven lookups can be computed in parallel



Each position keeps its own output \(z_i\), but that output may contain information gathered directly from every other position.


Unlike recurrence, self-attention creates direct token-to-token paths and computes all position-wise lookups in parallel (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Stack the seven lookups into matrices
text:
Stack the seven lookups into matrices

One row per token: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{7\times d_{model}}\).



INPUTS\(X\)\(7\times d_{model}\)


× \(W_Q\)× \(W_K\)× \(W_V\)



QUERIES\(Q\)\(7\times d_k\)


KEYS\(K\)\(7\times d_k\)


VALUES\(V\)\(7\times d_v\)



ALL QUERY–KEY SCORES\(S=QK^\top\)\(7\times7\)


ROW-WISE NORMALIZATION\(A=\operatorname{softmax}(S)\)each row sums to 1


ALL CONTEXTUAL OUTPUTS\(Z=AV\)\(7\times d_v\)



Row \(i\) of \(A\) contains the attention weights produced by token \(i\)’s query. Row \(i\) of \(Z\) is that token’s retrieved context.


Matrix multiplication computes every pairwise query–key score and every weighted value sum efficiently Vaswani et al. (2017); Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Self-attention shortens the information path


RECURRENT PATH

animal→→→→it

Information crosses several state updates.


SELF-ATTENTION PATH

animal⟶it

One learned connection can link distant tokens.




DIRECTAny position can reach any other in one attention step.


CONTEXTUALThe same token receives a different representation in a different sentence.


PARALLELAll queries can be evaluated together during training.



TWO QUESTIONS REMAIN How do we stop a language model from looking into the future? Can one similarity pattern capture every useful relationship?


Self-attention provides constant-length paths between positions, while its unrestricted all-to-all form introduces modeling and computational questions (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Larger vectors can create overconfident scores
text:
Larger vectors can create overconfident scores


ONE QUERY–KEY PAIR

\(q\)\([1,1,1,1]\)


\(k\)\([1,1,1,1]\)


\(q\cdot k=1+1+1+1=4\)



AS \(d_k\) GROWS

more coordinates⟶larger dot products⟶sharper softmax


A few large logits can push the distribution close to \(0\) or \(1\).




When softmax saturates, its gradients become small. We need the score scale to remain controlled as the key dimension grows.


Scaled dot-product attention compensates for growing dot-product magnitude at larger key dimensions (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: How much does scaling change the lookup?
text:
How much does scaling change the lookup?

PAUSE · GIVEN

SCORES[4, 2, 0]KEY DIMENSIONdk = 4

Compare the attention weights produced by:

UNSCALEDsoftmax([4, 2, 0])SCALEDsoftmax([4, 2, 0] ÷ √4)

Which distribution leaves more room for alternatives?

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Divide scores before softmax


WITHOUT SCALING\([4,2,0]\)

\(\downarrow\;\operatorname{softmax}\)


.87.12.02



SCALE\(\sqrt{d_k}=2\)


WITH SCALING\([2,1,0]\)

\(\downarrow\;\operatorname{softmax}\)


.67.24.09




\[\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\] Scaling preserves the ranking of keys—it prevents confidence from growing merely because vectors are wider.


The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor stabilizes dot-product scores before softmax (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: A language model must not read tomorrow
text:
A language model must not read tomorrow


POSITION 1The


POSITION 2animal


POSITION 3ran


POSITION 4home



To predict the token after “The animal ran”, unrestricted self-attention could inspect…“home”That would leak the answer during training.


At position \(i\), allow attention only to positions \(j\le i\).


Autoregressive language models enforce the left-to-right factorization with masked self-attention (Vaswani et al. 2017).

section: A causal mask closes every future connection
text:
A causal mask closes every future connection

1 · SCORES\(S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}\)


2 · ADD MASK\(\widetilde S=S+M\)future cells receive \(-\infty\)


3 · NORMALIZE\(A=\operatorname{softmax}(\widetilde S)\)future weights become exactly \(0\)




The computation stays parallel during training, but every prediction sees only its permitted past.


The triangular causal mask adds \(-\infty\) to forbidden logits before softmax Vaswani et al. (2017); Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer.

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
One pattern must decide what “matters”

Theanimaldidnotcrossthestreetbecauseitwaswide


For “it”, useful context may encode several relationships:



REFERENCEit → streetWhat does the pronoun denote?


DESCRIPTIONit → wideWhich property describes it?


PARTICIPANTSstreet ↔︎ animalWhich entities interact?



A single distribution can mix these signals. Multiple heads let the model perform several different lookups in parallel.


Head interpretations are illustrative rather than guaranteed; multi-head attention provides separate learned projection spaces (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Multiple heads perform parallel lookups


SAME INPUT\(X\)



HEAD 1\(\operatorname{Attn}(XW_1^Q,XW_1^K,XW_1^V)\)one learned similarity space


HEAD 2\(\operatorname{Attn}(XW_2^Q,XW_2^K,XW_2^V)\)another learned similarity space


HEAD \(h\)\(\operatorname{Attn}(XW_h^Q,XW_h^K,XW_h^V)\)learned independently



CONCATENATE + MIX\(\operatorname{Concat}(head_1,\ldots,head_h)W^O\)



Each head has its own \(W^Q\), \(W^K\), and \(W^V\). Their outputs are combined into one representation per token.


Multi-head attention projects queries, keys, and values several times, applies attention in parallel, then concatenates the results (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: The same sentence can be viewed in several ways
text:
The same sentence can be viewed in several ways

The animal did not cross the street because it was wide.

The heads do not receive different sentences. They learn different projections of the same input, retrieve different evidence, then combine their results.


This diagram illustrates the parallel learned subspaces of multi-head attention; individual linguistic roles are explanatory examples, not fixed assignments (Vaswani et al. 2017).

THE OPERATOR IS READY—BUT A MODEL IS NOT What must surround attention so tokens know their order and information can pass through many layers?


These mechanisms form the attention core of the Transformer; the surrounding architecture is the bridge to the next section (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Attention sees tokens—but where are their positions?
text:
Attention sees tokens—but where are their positions?


SENTENCE Adogbitesman


SENTENCE Bmanbitesdog



Both inputs contain the same three token embeddings. Self-attention receives no position index unless we provide one.



REORDER THE INPUTS\(PX\)

⟶

SELF-ATTENTION REORDERS ITS OUTPUTS\(P\,\operatorname{Attn}(X)\)



The model needs an explicit signal that distinguishes first, second, and third position.


Without positional information, self-attention is permutation equivariant: reordering inputs only reorders outputs (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
text:
Attention mixes positions—not features deeply

Attention answers “which positions should exchange information?” A complete layer must also answer “how should each position transform what it received?”


The Transformer pairs attention with a position-wise transformation; its construction is reserved for the next lecture (Vaswani et al. 2017).

title: Attention Mechanisms
section: Deep stacks need a safe information route
text:
Deep stacks need a safe information route


INPUT\(x\)


LAYER 1attention + transformation

AS DEPTH GROWS

Can the original representation survive?Can every layer train stably?



A practical architecture needs routes that preserve information and keep activations controlled—but we will build those routes next time.


Residual pathways and normalization make deep Transformer stacks trainable; this slide motivates rather than develops those mechanisms (Vaswani et al. 2017).

How do we assemble order, attention, transformation, and safe depth into one reusable block?

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Chapter 2 · Tokenization and embeddings
In the previous chapter, we treated “text” as if it could be handed directly to a model. It cannot. A model operates on numbers, so we need to make two decisions:
This chapter develops the main ideas and leaves most implementation details to the libraries that solve them well.
flowchart LR
    A[Raw text] --> B[Tokens]
    B --> C[Token IDs]
    C --> D[Vectors]
    D --> E[Model]

    B -. tokenization .-> B
    D -. embedding .-> D

    classDef raw fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef units fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef vectors fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a

Figure 1: Our journey: choose units, assign identifiers, then represent those units in a space where useful relationships can emerge.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
1.1 One string, several valid segmentations
What is the correct tokenization of don't?
["don't"]
["do", "n't"]
["don", "'", "t"]
["d", "o", "n", "'", "t"]
All four are mechanically possible. A linguistically informed system might preserve the contraction or separate its grammatical components. A subword model might choose reusable character sequences. A character model uses individual symbols.






Tokenization is not neutral cleanup. It determines the units the model can see, the vocabulary it must store, and the length of every input.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
1.2 Token, type, and vocabulary
In the sentence:

A model is a model.

there are six word/punctuation tokens, but fewer distinct types because a and model occur twice. A vocabulary contains types; an input contains token instances.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
4.1 The intuition behind byte-pair encoding
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts with small units and repeatedly merges frequent neighboring pairs (Sennrich et al. 2016).






flowchart LR
    A["l o w e r"] -->|merge l + o| B["lo w e r"]
    B -->|merge lo + w| C["low e r"]
    C -->|merge e + r| D["low er"]
    D --> E["vocabulary includes: low, er"]

    classDef stage fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef result fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A,B,C,D stage
    class E result




Figure 5: A simplified BPE story: frequent adjacent units become reusable vocabulary entries.





We only need the principle today. The complete learning algorithm and its alternatives belong to a deeper treatment of model construction.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
4.2 Names you will encounter

BPE: merges frequent adjacent units (Sennrich et al. 2016).
WordPiece: grows a vocabulary using a likelihood-based criterion rather than raw pair frequency (Schuster and Nakajima 2012).
Unigram: begins with many candidate pieces and removes those whose absence least harms the segmentation likelihood (Kudo 2018).
SentencePiece: trains directly from raw text and treats whitespace explicitly (Kudo and Richardson 2018).
Byte-level subwords: begin from a fixed byte vocabulary, guaranteeing coverage, then merge byte sequences for greater efficiency (Wang et al. 2019).

Different algorithms and vocabularies split the same text differently. A tokenizer is therefore part of its model—not a detachable generic preprocessing step.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
5.1 A deliberately small regular-expression tokenizer
Regular expressions are useful when the task has a small, explicit token definition.
import re

TOKEN_PATTERN = r"\b\w+(?:['’]\w+)?\b|[^\w\s]"

text = "NLP isn't just words—it includes punctuation!"
tokens = re.findall(TOKEN_PATTERN, text)
print(tokens)
['NLP', "isn't", 'just', 'words', '—', 'it', 'includes', 'punctuation', '!']
This is readable and testable, but it is not a universal tokenizer. URLs, abbreviations, emoji sequences, scripts without whitespace, and language-specific conventions quickly require more care.






TipWhat the expression says






\b\w+ begins with one or more word characters.
(?:['’]\w+)? optionally preserves an apostrophe followed by more word characters.
| means “or.”
[^\w\s] captures a remaining symbol that is neither a word character nor whitespace.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
5.2 A linguistic tokenizer with spaCy
spaCy combines general rules with language-specific exceptions for forms such as contractions, abbreviations, punctuation, URLs, and email addresses (Explosion 2026).
import spacy

nlp = spacy.blank("en")
examples = [
    "Apple is buying a U.K. startup for $1.2 billion.",
    "Don't email support@example.com—visit https://example.com.",
]

for text in examples:
    print([token.text for token in nlp(text)])
The useful classroom question is not merely whether the output “looks right.” Ask which rule produced each boundary and whether those boundaries suit the downstream task.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
5.3 A pretrained model tokenizer
Hugging Face’s AutoTokenizer loads the exact tokenizer associated with a pretrained model (Hugging Face 2026).
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-multilingual-cased")

examples = [
    "Tokenization is surprisingly complicated.",
    "La tokenisation dépend du modèle.",
    "الترميز يعتمد على النموذج.",
]

for text in examples:
    pieces = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    ids = tokenizer(text, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
    print(text)
    print(pieces)
    print(ids)






flowchart LR
    A[Text] --> B[Normalization]
    B --> C[Pre-tokenization]
    C --> D[Subword model]
    D --> E[Special tokens]
    E --> F[Token IDs]
    F -->|decode| G[Text]

    classDef input fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef process fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef output fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a

    class B,C,D,E process

Figure 6: A modern tokenizer performs several coordinated operations and can reverse IDs back into text.











Never pair a model with a different tokenizer merely because both accept text. Token IDs only have meaning relative to the vocabulary and embedding table used during that model’s training.

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
7.1 Measuring similarity
Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors rather than their absolute length:
\[
\operatorname{cosine}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
= \frac{\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}}
{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}.
\]
Values near 1 indicate similar directions; values near 0 indicate little directional relationship.
similarity(cat, dog)  >  similarity(cat, democracy)

title: From Text to Meaning
text:
7.2 The classical analogy
A famous demonstration uses vector arithmetic:
\[
\mathbf{king} - \mathbf{man} + \mathbf{woman} \approx \mathbf{queen}.
\]
The relation from man to woman is approximately repeated from king to queen. This is an illuminating regularity, not a universal algebra of meaning. Results depend on the corpus, algorithm, vocabulary, and similarity rule—and the same space can encode harmful social stereotypes.






flowchart LR
    M[man] -->|relationship| W[woman]
    K[king] -->|similar displacement| Q[queen]
    M -. subtract .-> K
    W -. add .-> Q

    classDef royal fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class M,W base
    class K,Q royal

section: 8.1 Plot a small part of the embedding space
text:
8.1 Plot a small part of the embedding space
We cannot directly draw 100 dimensions. Principal component analysis (PCA) projects the selected vectors into two dimensions for inspection.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

words = [
    "king", "queen", "prince", "princess",
    "man", "woman", "boy", "girl",
    "cat", "dog", "paris", "france",
]

matrix = vectors[words]
points = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(matrix)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], color="#0f6f78")

for word, (x, y) in zip(words, points):
    ax.annotate(word, (x, y), xytext=(5, 4), textcoords="offset points")

ax.axhline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_title("A two-dimensional PCA projection of selected GloVe vectors")
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component 1")
ax.set_ylabel("Principal component 2")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()






PCA preserves directions of greatest variance, not every pairwise distance. Moving the selected words can change the projection. Always verify claims with similarities in the original embedding space.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Chapter 3 · Learning word embeddings
In Chapter 2, we used pretrained vectors as if their coordinates had simply appeared. Related words were nearby, cosine similarity measured their closeness, and vector arithmetic sometimes recovered familiar relationships. This chapter asks the missing question:
The central answer is surprisingly economical: use context as supervision. A corpus does not explicitly say that coffee and tea are related, but both occur near words such as drink, cup, hot, and morning. Embedding algorithms turn those repeated contextual patterns into geometry.
flowchart LR
    A[Text corpus] --> B[Context windows]
    B --> C[Co-occurrence signal]
    C --> D[Learning objective]
    D --> E[Dense vectors]
    E --> F[Similarity and analogy]

    classDef data fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef learn fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef result fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A,B data
    class C,D learn
    class E,F result




Figure 1: The chapter’s central path: context supplies the training signal from which a useful geometry emerges.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
1.1 One-hot vectors keep words separate
A one-hot vector gives every vocabulary item its own coordinate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{apple}  &\rightarrow [1,0,0,0],\\
\text{orange} &\rightarrow [0,1,0,0],\\
\text{car}    &\rightarrow [0,0,1,0],\\
\text{bus}    &\rightarrow [0,0,0,1].
\end{aligned}
\]
This representation avoids pretending that vocabulary indices have numerical order. It also creates a new problem: all distinct words are equally dissimilar.
For any two different one-hot vectors \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\),
\[
\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rVert_2=\sqrt{2}.
\]
The representation knows that apple and orange are different, but not that both are fruit.



Table 1: Three ways of representing vocabulary items.





Representation

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 1.2 Dense vectors can express graded relationships
text:
1.2 Dense vectors can express graded relationships
An embedding assigns a short, dense vector to each word. For illustration, imagine a learned two-dimensional space:
apple  → [0.82, 0.16]
orange → [0.79, 0.22]
car    → [0.11, 0.85]
bus    → [0.16, 0.80]
The coordinate names are not usually known. What matters is their relationship: fruit vectors point in similar directions, as do vehicle vectors.






An embedding is useful because of the geometry of the collection, not because one coordinate has an obvious human-readable definition.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
2.1 Euclidean distance
Euclidean distance measures the straight-line separation between two points:
\[
d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = \lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\rVert_2.
\]
Smaller values mean closer points. This is intuitive, but vector length can affect the result.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
2.2 Dot product
The dot product is
\[
\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}u_i v_i.
\]
It becomes large when two vectors align and have substantial magnitude. Word2Vec uses dot products as trainable compatibility scores.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
2.3 Cosine similarity
Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both vector lengths:
\[
\operatorname{cos}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
=\frac{\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}}
{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert_2\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert_2}.
\tag{1}\]
It asks whether the vectors point in similar directions. It is the standard first choice when querying static word embeddings.
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(u, v):
    u = np.asarray(u, dtype=float)
    v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)
    return np.dot(u, v) / (np.linalg.norm(u) * np.linalg.norm(v))

apple = [0.82, 0.16]
orange = [0.79, 0.22]
car = [0.11, 0.85]

print(cosine_similarity(apple, orange))
print(cosine_similarity(apple, car))






WarningSimilarity is not identity



Nearest neighbors can be synonyms, but they can also be related concepts, grammatical alternatives, or opposites. Hot and cold occur in many of the same contexts and may therefore be close.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
2.4 The classical analogy
The most famous word-vector demonstration is
\[
\mathbf{king}-\mathbf{man}+\mathbf{woman}\approx\mathbf{queen}.
\]
It suggests that some relations correspond approximately to directions in the space. We search for the word whose vector has the greatest cosine similarity to the result.






flowchart LR
    M[man] -->|gender direction| W[woman]
    K[king] -->|similar direction| Q[queen]
    M -. royalty direction .-> K
    W -. royalty direction .-> Q

    classDef common fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef royal fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class M,W common
    class K,Q royal




Figure 2: A word analogy asks whether two pairs exhibit approximately parallel displacements.





This is a memorable illustration, not a law of language. Analogy results depend on the corpus, algorithm, vocabulary, and search procedure.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
3.1 What counts as context?
Context is a modeling decision. It might mean:

neighboring words within a fixed window;
all words in the same sentence or document;
words connected by a grammatical dependency; or
documents, users, or time periods associated with a word.

Classical Word2Vec normally uses a short window around each word. A narrow window often emphasizes functional similarity; a wider window can emphasize topical relatedness.
For the sentence
the curious student reads the book
with a window radius of two, the center word student has these context words:
the curious [student] reads the
 ↑     ↑                 ↑    ↑
context                 context
The ordered center–context pairs are:
(student, the)
(student, curious)
(student, reads)
(student, the)
Repeating this operation across a large corpus creates millions or billions of weak training examples without manual labels.






TipCorpus text supervises itself



No annotator labels two words as semantically related. Their observed neighborhoods supply the signal. This is an early and influential form of self-supervised learning.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
4.1 Constructing a matrix in Python
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np

sentences = [
    "cats chase mice".split(),
    "dogs chase cats".split(),
    "dogs eat food".split(),
    "cats eat food".split(),
]

vocabulary = sorted({word for sentence in sentences for word in sentence})
word_to_id = {word: i for i, word in enumerate(vocabulary)}
counts = np.zeros((len(vocabulary), len(vocabulary)), dtype=int)

window = 1
for sentence in sentences:
    for center_index, center in enumerate(sentence):
        left = max(0, center_index - window)
        right = min(len(sentence), center_index + window + 1)
        for context_index in range(left, right):
            if context_index == center_index:
                continue
            context = sentence[context_index]
            counts[word_to_id[center], word_to_id[context]] += 1

print(vocabulary)
print(counts)

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 4.2 Why raw counts are not enough
text:
4.2 Why raw counts are not enough
Raw co-occurrence matrices have three major limitations:

They are huge and sparse. A vocabulary of 100,000 words produces \(10^{10}\) possible cells.
Frequency dominates. Common function words occur with almost everything.
Counts do not distinguish expected from surprising co-occurrence. Ten observations may be informative for rare words but ordinary for frequent ones.

Pointwise mutual information compares observed co-occurrence with what independence would predict:
\[
\operatorname{PMI}(w,c)
=\log\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)}.
\tag{2}\]
A positive value means that \(w\) and \(c\) occur together more often than chance would suggest. Positive PMI (PPMI) replaces negative values with zero.






NoteHistorical route: matrix reduction





Classical distributional methods can weight a word–context matrix and compress it with a technique such as singular value decomposition. This is an important historical route to dense representations, but it is not our focus. We now turn to methods that learn the vectors directly from a predictive or count-based objective.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
5.1 Step 1: create positive pairs
For a token sequence \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) and window radius \(m\), Skip-gram creates \((w_t,w_{t+j})\) pairs for \(-m\leq j\leq m\), excluding \(j=0\) and positions outside the sentence.
def skipgram_pairs(tokens, window_size=2):
    pairs = []
    for center_index, center in enumerate(tokens):
        left = max(0, center_index - window_size)
        right = min(len(tokens), center_index + window_size + 1)

        for context_index in range(left, right):
            if context_index != center_index:
                pairs.append((center, tokens[context_index]))
    return pairs

tokens = "the curious student reads the book".split()
print(skipgram_pairs(tokens, window_size=2))
Every observed pair receives the label \(1\): it is a positive example.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 5.2 Step 2: store two vectors per word
text:
5.2 Step 2: store two vectors per word
Skip-gram maintains two parameter matrices:
\[
W_{\text{center}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
W_{\text{context}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d}.
\]
Selecting word \(w\) from the first matrix gives its center vector \(\mathbf{v}_w\). Selecting context \(c\) from the second gives \(\mathbf{u}_c\).






flowchart LR
    A[center word ID] --> B[center embedding table]
    B --> C[center vector v]
    D[context word ID] --> E[context embedding table]
    E --> F[context vector u]
    C --> G[dot product]
    F --> G
    G --> H[compatibility score]

    classDef input fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef param fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef score fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A,D input
    class B,C,E,F param
    class G,H score




Figure 3: Skip-gram looks up a center vector and scores it against a context vector.





Conceptually, a one-hot word vector multiplied by an embedding matrix selects a row. Software performs this operation efficiently as a lookup rather than a full matrix multiplication.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
5.3 Step 3: score a pair
The dot product
\[
s(w,c)=\mathbf{u}_c^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_w
\]
scores compatibility. A sigmoid converts the score to a number between zero and one:
\[
\sigma(s)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-s}}.
\]
For an observed pair, training should make \(\sigma(\mathbf{u}_c^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_w)\) large.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 5.4 Why not predict every vocabulary word?
text:
5.4 Why not predict every vocabulary word?
The original full prediction view assigns a probability to every possible context word:
\[
P(c\mid w)=
\frac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_c^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_w)}
{\sum_{c'\in V}\exp(\mathbf{u}_{c'}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}_w)}.
\]
The denominator examines the entire vocabulary for every training pair. With millions of pairs and a large vocabulary, that is expensive.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
6.1 The learning loop






flowchart LR
    A[Select center word] --> B[Collect nearby positive contexts]
    B --> C[Sample negative contexts]
    C --> D[Look up center and context vectors]
    D --> E[Compute dot-product scores]
    E --> F[Compute binary loss]
    F --> G[Update embedding tables]
    G -. next pair .-> A

    classDef data fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef learn fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    class A,B,C data
    class D,E,F,G learn




Figure 4: The Skip-gram learning loop repeats simple local decisions across a large corpus.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
6.2 A compact PyTorch model
This model shows the central computation without implementing a complete training pipeline:
import torch
from torch import nn

class SkipGramNegativeSampling(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocabulary_size, embedding_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.center_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)
        self.context_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)

    def forward(self, center_ids, context_ids):
        center_vectors = self.center_embeddings(center_ids)
        context_vectors = self.context_embeddings(context_ids)
        return (center_vectors * context_vectors).sum(dim=-1)

model = SkipGramNegativeSampling(vocabulary_size=10_000, embedding_dim=100)

# Each position represents one positive or sampled-negative pair.
center_ids = torch.tensor([12, 12, 12, 12])
context_ids = torch.tensor([98, 401, 57, 806])
labels = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])

scores = model(center_ids, context_ids)
loss = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(scores, labels)
loss.backward()
binary_cross_entropy_with_logits combines the sigmoid and binary loss in a numerically stable operation.






NoteWhat happens to the two embedding tables?





Word2Vec trains separate center and context matrices. Implementations may publish the center vectors, the context vectors, or a combination. This choice can change evaluation results. “The Word2Vec vector” is therefore shorthand for a representation extracted from the trained parameters.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
6.3 CBOW in one picture
Continuous Bag of Words reverses the task:
Skip-gram:  student → curious, reads, the, ...
CBOW:       the + curious + reads + the → student
CBOW combines nearby context vectors—often by averaging—and predicts the center word. It is usually faster; Skip-gram often represents infrequent words better. The deeper lesson is shared: prediction forces the embedding table to organize itself around distributional evidence.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
7.1 Co-occurrence ratios carry information
Imagine comparing the contexts ice and steam:

\(P(k\mid\text{ice})\)
\(P(k\mid\text{steam})\)

The contrast between two co-occurrence profiles can reveal semantic relationships more clearly than either raw count alone.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
7.2 The GloVe objective
Let \(X_{ij}\) be the number of times word \(j\) occurs in the context of word \(i\). GloVe learns word vectors \(\mathbf{w}_i\), context vectors \(\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_j\), and biases by minimizing
\[
J=\sum_{i,j}f(X_{ij})
\left(
\mathbf{w}_i^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_j
+b_i+\widetilde{b}_j-\log X_{ij}
\right)^2.
\tag{4}\]
Read the equation in pieces:

\(X_{ij}\) records global co-occurrence.
The vector dot product plus biases predicts \(\log X_{ij}\).
The squared error penalizes poor predictions.
The weighting function \(f\) prevents extremely rare and extremely frequent pairs from dominating.

The logarithm compresses the enormous range of corpus counts. The weighting function trusts informative counts while limiting the influence of very frequent pairs.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
7.3 Word2Vec and GloVe compared



Table 5: Word2Vec and GloVe use different objectives but exploit the same distributional evidence.










Property
Word2Vec Skip-gram
GloVe




Immediate training signal
Local center–context pairs
Aggregated co-occurrence counts


Typical objective
Distinguish observed from sampled pairs
Reconstruct log co-occurrence


Uses global corpus statistics
Indirectly, through repeated sampling
Explicitly


Produces
Static dense word vectors
Static dense word vectors


Main intuition

Do not reduce the comparison to “neural versus count-based.” Both methods learn parameters with optimization, and both are closely connected to transformed co-occurrence statistics. Their difference lies mainly in how the corpus evidence enters the objective.

8.1 Well-known static embeddings



Table 6: Three influential families of pretrained static word embeddings.











Family

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
8.2 Query GloVe with Gensim
import gensim.downloader as api

vectors = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")

print(vectors.similarity("coffee", "tea"))
print(vectors.similarity("coffee", "airplane"))
print(vectors.most_similar("language", topn=5))

analogy = vectors.most_similar(
    positive=["king", "woman"],
    negative=["man"],
    topn=5,
)
print(analogy)
The first download can take time; later calls use Gensim’s local cache. Exact neighbors vary across models.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
8.3 Use vectors through spaCy
spaCy is not an embedding algorithm. It is an NLP library whose medium and large pipelines include pretrained static vectors. This makes it useful for applied exploration.
python -m spacy download en_core_web_md
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_md")

coffee = nlp.vocab["coffee"]
tea = nlp.vocab["tea"]
airplane = nlp.vocab["airplane"]

print(coffee.has_vector, coffee.vector.shape)
print(coffee.similarity(tea))
print(coffee.similarity(airplane))






The small English pipeline, en_core_web_sm, does not include a full table of static word vectors. Use en_core_web_md or en_core_web_lg for this exercise.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
8.4 Inspect neighborhoods, not isolated scores
A similarity value becomes meaningful only through comparison. Ask several questions:

Are obvious related words near one another?
Are the neighbors synonyms, topical associates, or grammatical alternatives?
Does the behavior change for rare words or names?
Does the model work equally well for the languages and domains you need?

for query in ["doctor", "computer", "beautiful", "running"]:
    print(query, vectors.most_similar(query, topn=5))

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
8.5 Visualize a small selection carefully
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

words = [
    "king", "queen", "prince", "princess",
    "coffee", "tea", "juice", "water",
    "car", "bus", "train", "bicycle",
]

points = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(vectors[words])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], color="#0f6f78")

for word, (x, y) in zip(words, points):
    ax.annotate(word, (x, y), xytext=(5, 4), textcoords="offset points")

ax.set_title("PCA projection of selected GloVe vectors")
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component 1")
ax.set_ylabel("Principal component 2")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
PCA creates a lossy two-dimensional projection. Similarities should be calculated in the original 100-dimensional space, not inferred only from the picture.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
9.1 One word, one vector
A static vocabulary stores one vector for bank, whether the sentence refers to money or a river:
She deposited money at the bank.
They sat on the river bank.
The learned vector blends evidence from both senses. A contextual model instead produces a representation conditioned on the surrounding sentence.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
9.2 Corpus boundaries become model boundaries
An embedding can only reflect evidence available in its training data. Specialized terminology, recent events, dialects, and underrepresented languages may be poorly represented. Similarity is learned from a corpus, not discovered as an objective fact.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
text:
9.3 Frequency and vocabulary remain important
Rare words receive fewer reliable updates. Word-level models cannot construct a vector for an unseen spelling. fastText reduces this problem with character \(n\)-grams, but it does not eliminate missing knowledge.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 9.4 Bias is part of the geometry
text:
9.4 Bias is part of the geometry
Corpora contain historical and social stereotypes. Distributional learning can encode those associations and reproduce them in nearest neighbors and analogies (Bolukbasi et al. 2016). The same geometric regularities that make embeddings useful can make them harmful.






An embedding measures patterns of usage in a corpus. It does not provide a neutral dictionary of human meaning.

title: Learning Word Embeddings
section: 9.5 Intrinsic success is not task success
text:
9.5 Intrinsic success is not task success
Word similarities and analogies are intrinsic evaluations: they test the representation directly. The more important question is often extrinsic: does the representation improve a real classifier, search system, or other downstream task?

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing
Chapter 5 · Neural networks for sequences
A fixed-window language model can use several recent words, but it cannot decide to remember an important word for an unknown amount of time. This chapter develops the machinery needed to replace that rigid window with a learned state. We will move from neural language models to recurrent computation, backpropagation through time, gated memory, and finally sequence-to-sequence learning.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: 1.1 A dependency that does not fit the window
text:
1.1 A dependency that does not fit the window
Keep the following sentence visible throughout the example:

The keys to the cabinet ___ on the table.

The exact task is to predict the missing verb. The plural noun keys determines that the correct continuation is are. The singular noun cabinet is closer to the blank, but it is not the subject.
The token sequence available before the prediction is:



Table 1: The important grammatical feature occurs at position 2, while the nearest noun occurs at position 5.

A bigram model retains only the final token:
\[
P(w_6\mid w_{1:5})
\approx
P(w_6\mid \text{cabinet}).
\]
The model therefore asks, “Which word often follows cabinet?” It cannot ask, “Which verb agrees with the subject of this clause?” The plural feature was present in the sentence, but it was discarded before prediction.

ImportantTry it before reading the solution



Suppose the model is a trigram. Its retained history contains two tokens.

What exact history does it see before predicting the verb?
Does that history contain the number of the subject?
What minimum n-gram order would include keys in this particular sentence?




1.1.1 Worked solution
The two-token trigram history is:
the cabinet
It still does not contain keys, so it does not expose the subject’s plural number. The distance from keys to the missing verb is four token transitions:
keys → to → the → cabinet → ___
To include keys when predicting the blank, the retained history must contain four tokens. That requires a 5-gram model:
\[
P(w_6\mid w_{1:5})
\approx
P(w_6\mid w_2,w_3,w_4,w_5).
\]
For this one sentence, increasing the order repairs the missing-input problem. It does not provide a general solution: another sentence can insert five, ten, or fifty tokens between the subject and its verb.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: 1.2 Why increasing the order is not learned memory
text:
1.2 Why increasing the order is not learned memory
Increasing \(n\) changes the length of the window, not the rule used to select information. The model still retains a fixed suffix and discards the rest.
If the vocabulary contains \(|V|\) tokens, an order-\(n\) model may need to distinguish as many as \(|V|^{n-1}\) histories and \(|V|^n\) complete n-grams. For \(|V|=50{,}000\),
\[
(50{,}000)^5
= 3.125\times 10^{23}
\]
possible 5-grams exist.
The number is not a claim that a system will store a dense table of that size. It exposes the combinatorial space in which observations become sparse: longer histories are more informative when repeated, but exact repetitions become less likely (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: 1.3 Two limitations that should not be confused
text:
1.3 Two limitations that should not be confused
N-gram models exhibit two related but distinct failures.

1.3.1 Failure 1: sparse evidence
Suppose the training corpus contains:

the cat rested

but never contains:

the dog rested

A count model may assign the second phrase zero probability even though cat and dog occur in similar linguistic environments. This is a generalization problem: the model treats different word identities as unrelated table entries.
Smoothing redistributes probability mass and prevents unseen events from receiving probability zero. However, ordinary smoothing still does not give cat and dog a learned geometric relationship.


1.3.2 Failure 2: discarded evidence
In the agreement sentence, the relevant word keys occurred, but it fell outside the active window. This is a memory problem: information needed at prediction time is absent from the model input.
Smoothing cannot reconstruct a feature that the representation has already removed. The difference can be summarized as follows:



Table 3: Generalization and memory require different repairs.










Question
Sparse evidence
Discarded evidence




Was the useful information in the active representation?
Yes, but the event was rare or unseen
No


Typical symptom
zero or unreliable count
prediction based on the wrong local cue


Can smoothing help?
Yes
No


Needed architectural change
share evidence across similar words
carry selected information across time












WarningCommon misconception



“Use a larger n” is not a mechanism for long-term memory. It is a decision to preserve a longer fixed suffix, with a rapidly growing and increasingly sparse context space.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
1.4 Section synthesis
An n-gram model forgets by position: once a token leaves the window, its information is unavailable. A useful sequence model should instead learn a compact representation that:

shares statistical evidence across related words;
is updated as each new token arrives;
preserves information when it remains useful; and
discards information when it no longer matters.

The first neural step will address the generalization problem by replacing symbolic word identities with learned vectors and shared parameters. It will also make the remaining memory limitation easier to see.






ImportantQuestion leading to the next section



Can a neural language model learn that cat and dog are similar while keeping the exact inputs, vectors, and scores inspectable?

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
2.1 Bengio’s distributed-representation argument
Consider two contexts:
the cat rested
the dog rested
A count table stores separate entries for cat and dog. A neural model instead looks up learned embeddings
\[
\mathbf e_{\text{cat}}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{cat}},
\qquad
\mathbf e_{\text{dog}}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{dog}},
\]
where \(C\in\mathbb R^{d_e\times |V|}\) is an embedding matrix and each one-hot vector selects one column. If training makes the two embeddings nearby, then a shared downstream network reacts similarly to both words.






TipWhat is being shared?



The model does not copy a probability from one sentence to another. It learns reusable features. A hidden unit that responds to “animate subject” or “plural noun” can fire for many words instead of requiring a separate count for every surface form.


The original neural probabilistic language model jointly learned word vectors and the probability function that used them. Its architecture is reproduced in Figure 4 for historical reference.






Figure 4: The neural probabilistic language-model architecture. Reproduced from Bengio et al. (2003), Fig. 1.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: 2.2 Building the model from inspectable objects
text:
2.2 Building the model from inspectable objects
Use a four-word context to predict the next word:
the students opened their  →  ?
Let every embedding have dimension \(d_e\). The model constructs four visible objects.

2.2.1 1. Look up one vector per context word
\[
\mathbf e^{(1)}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{the}},\quad
\mathbf e^{(2)}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{students}},\quad
\mathbf e^{(3)}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{opened}},\quad
\mathbf e^{(4)}=C\mathbf 1_{\text{their}}.
\]
The same matrix \(C\) performs every lookup. Word identity chooses a column; position does not create a new embedding table.


2.2.2 2. Concatenate the window
\[
\mathbf x=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf e^{(1)}\\
\mathbf e^{(2)}\\
\mathbf e^{(3)}\\
\mathbf e^{(4)}
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^{4d_e}.
\tag{2}\]
Concatenation preserves word order because each position occupies a different block of \(mathbf x\).


2.2.3 3. Compute a hidden representation
\[
\mathbf a=W\mathbf x+\mathbf b_h,
\qquad
\mathbf h=\tanh(\mathbf a),
\tag{3}\]
with \(W\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times 4d_e}\) and \(mathbf b_h\in\mathbb R^{d_h}\).


2.2.4 4. Produce a vocabulary distribution
\[
\mathbf z=U\mathbf h+\mathbf b_o,
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf y}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z),
\tag{4}\]
where \(U\in\mathbb R^{|V|\times d_h}\). The output contains one probability per vocabulary item. Plausible continuations might include books and laptops; implausible continuations remain present with low probability.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
section: 2.3 What the neural window fixes—and what it does not
text:
2.3 What the neural window fixes—and what it does not
The neural model improves generalization in two ways:

embeddings allow related words to share evidence; and
shared matrices replace a table containing one independent parameter set per observed n-gram.

The memory policy, however, remains fixed. If the window contains \(k\) embeddings,
\[
\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{kd_e},
\qquad
W\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times kd_e}.
\]
Adding one more position adds \(d_hd_e\) parameters to \(W\). More importantly, concatenation assigns a distinct block of \(W\) to every position. The model does not apply one position-independent rule repeatedly through time.






WarningThe boundary moved; it did not disappear



A four-word neural window forgets the fifth-most-recent word just as completely as a 5-gram model. Distributed representations repair exact-match generalization, not unbounded memory.


The required architecture should accept an arbitrary number of inputs while keeping its parameter shapes fixed. That requirement leads to recurrence.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
3.1 One recurrent cell
For input \(mathbf x_t\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\) and previous state \(mathbf h_{t-1}\in\mathbb R^{d_h}\), a simple tanh RNN computes
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf a_t &= W_x\mathbf x_t+W_h\mathbf h_{t-1}+\mathbf b_h,\\
\mathbf h_t &= \tanh(\mathbf a_t),\\
\mathbf z_t &= U\mathbf h_t+\mathbf b_o,\\
\hat{\mathbf y}_t &= \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z_t).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
The matrices have fixed shapes:
\[
W_x\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_x},\quad
W_h\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_h},\quad
U\in\mathbb R^{|V|\times d_h}.
\]
The subscript \(t\) appears on activations, not parameters. Every time step reuses \(W_x\), \(W_h\), \(U\), and the biases.






NoteState is not a stored sentence



\(\mathbf h_t\) is a learned summary produced by repeated transformations. It is not a list of previous words, and no coordinate is guaranteed to have a human-readable meaning. Training determines which aspects of the history become useful features.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
3.2 A complete scalar forward pass
Before working with vectors, inspect a one-dimensional RNN. Let
\[
h_t=\tanh(w_xx_t+w_hh_{t-1}+b),
\]
with
\[
w_x=0.8,\qquad w_h=0.5,\qquad b=0,\qquad h_0=0.
\]
Suppose two scalar inputs are \(x_1=1\) and \(x_2=-0.5\).






ImportantTry it first



Compute \(a_1,h_1,a_2,h_2\). Keep at least three decimal places.


At the first step,
\[
a_1=0.8(1)+0.5(0)=0.8,
\qquad
h_1=\tanh(0.8)\approx0.664.
\]
At the second step, the new input and previous state meet:
\[
a_2=0.8(-0.5)+0.5(0.664)
=-0.400+0.332=-0.068,
\]
\[
h_2=\tanh(-0.068)\approx-0.068.
\]



Table 5: The state combines new evidence with a transformed summary of earlier evidence.
