The state can continue for five or five hundred inputs without changing the number or shapes of the parameters. The price is sequential computation: \(h_t\) cannot be computed until \(h_{t-1}\) exists.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
4.1 Backpropagation through one cell
For a one-hot target \(\mathbf y_t\), the cross-entropy loss is
\[
J^{(t)}=-\sum_{v\in V}y_{t,v}\log\hat y_{t,v}.
\tag{6}\]
Softmax and cross-entropy simplify the derivative with respect to logits:
\[
\boldsymbol\delta_{z,t}
=\frac{\partial J^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf z_t}
=\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t.
\tag{7}\]
The output matrix sends that error into hidden-state space:
\[
\mathbf g_{h,t}^{\text{local}}
=U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_{z,t}.
\]
For \(\mathbf h_t=\tanh(\mathbf a_t)\),
\[
\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t}
=\mathbf g_{h,t}\odot(1-\mathbf h_t\odot\mathbf h_t).
\tag{8}\]
The same pre-activation error produces every parameter gradient entering the cell:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial J}{\partial W_x}&=\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t}\mathbf x_t^\top,\\
\frac{\partial J}{\partial W_h}&=\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t}\mathbf h_{t-1}^\top,\\
\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf b_h}&=\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t},\\
\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf h_{t-1}}&=W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]
The final line is what makes temporal credit assignment possible: error at time \(t\) becomes an error signal for the preceding state.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
4.2 One concrete token loss
After the context
the students opened their
suppose the observed target is books and the model assigns
\[
\hat y_{t,\text{books}}=0.62.
\]
Because the target is one-hot, all terms in Equation 6 except the target entry vanish:
\[
J^{(t)}=-\log(0.62)\approx0.478.
\]
A larger probability on the correct word produces a smaller loss. The loss is attached to this output, but its gradient reaches the state, the current input path, and the preceding state.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
4.3 Multiple gradient paths add
An intermediate state \(\mathbf h_t\) has at least two downstream uses:

it produces the current output and loss \(J^{(t)}\); and
it influences \(\mathbf h_{t+1}\) and therefore all later losses.

Backpropagation sums both contributions:
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf h_t}
=
\underbrace{U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_{z,t}}_{\text{current output}}
+
\underbrace{W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t+1}}_{\text{future recurrence}}.
\tag{10}\]
This is an application of the multivariable chain rule. Backpropagation does not choose one route through a graph; every downstream route contributes to the gradient of a shared node.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
4.4 Backpropagation through time
For a sequence with \(T\) supervised outputs, the total objective is often a sum or mean of token losses:
\[
J=\sum_{t=1}^{T}J^{(t)}.
\tag{11}\]
Backpropagation through time (BPTT) means:

unfold the recurrent computation over the observed sequence;
compute all token losses;
propagate gradients backward from later states to earlier states; and
sum every time-step contribution to the shared parameters.







flowchart LR
    L1[J1] --> H1[h1]
    L2[J2] --> H2[h2]
    L3[J3] --> H3[h3]
    H3 -. gradient .-> H2
    H2 -. gradient .-> H1
    H1 --> P[shared gradients]
    H2 --> P
    H3 --> P

    classDef loss fill:#f8e5df,stroke:#d95f43,color:#17364a
    classDef state fill:#ffffff,stroke:#356fa8,color:#17364a
    classDef params fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    class L1,L2,L3 loss
    class H1,H2,H3 state
    class P params




Figure 6: Each time step uses the same parameters, so its local contribution is added to one shared parameter gradient.





For example,
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial W_h}
=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol\delta_{a,t}\mathbf h_{t-1}^{\top}.
\tag{12}\]
The sum reflects weight sharing: there are many uses of \(W_h\), but only one parameter tensor to update.






TipImplementation view



Modern automatic-differentiation systems construct this unfolded computation graph dynamically or symbolically. “Run BPTT” usually means computing the forward sequence loss and calling the framework’s backward operation—not manually writing every derivative.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
6.1 The repeated Jacobian product
For the simple RNN,
\[
\frac{\partial\mathbf h_t}{\partial\mathbf h_{t-1}}
=D_tW_h,
\]
where
\[
D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1-\mathbf h_t\odot\mathbf h_t)
\]
contains derivatives of tanh. A gradient traveling from time \(T\) to time \(0\) contains
\[
\frac{\partial\mathbf h_T}{\partial\mathbf h_0}
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}D_tW_h.
\tag{13}\]
If these local transformations repeatedly contract the signal, the gradient vanishes. If they repeatedly expand it, the gradient explodes (Bengio et al. 1994; Pascanu et al. 2013).

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
6.2 A scalar calculation
The matrix case changes different directions by different amounts, but a scalar chain exposes the basic behavior.






ImportantTry it first



A loss gradient has magnitude \(1\) at the final state and crosses four identical local derivatives.

What reaches the first state if every derivative is \(0.6\)?
What reaches it if every derivative is \(1.5\)?



For the contracting case,
\[
1\times0.6^4=0.1296.
\]
The successive magnitudes are
1.000 → 0.600 → 0.360 → 0.216 → 0.1296
For the expanding case,
\[
1\times1.5^4=5.0625,
\]
with
1.000 → 1.500 → 2.250 → 3.375 → 5.0625



Table 6: Both behaviors arise from repeated local transformations, not from sequence length alone.









Behavior
Training consequence




Vanishing gradient
early states receive almost no learning signal from distant losses


Exploding gradient
updates become unstable and may overflow numerically

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
6.3 Gradient clipping: a practical guardrail
Clipping by global norm caps an excessively large gradient while preserving its direction. Given gradient vector \(mathbf g\) and threshold \(\tau\),
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf g}
=\min\left(1,\frac{\tau}{\lVert\mathbf g\rVert_2}\right)\mathbf g.
\tag{14}\]
If \(\lVert\mathbf g\rVert_2=18\) and \(\tau=5\),
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf g}=\frac{5}{18}\mathbf g,
\qquad
\lVert\widetilde{\mathbf g}\rVert_2=5.
\]
Every component is multiplied by the same positive scalar, so the direction is unchanged.
def clip_by_global_norm(gradient, threshold):
    norm = gradient.norm(p=2)
    if norm > threshold:
        gradient = (threshold / norm) * gradient
    return gradient






WarningWhat clipping does not solve



Clipping controls explosions. It cannot restore a long-range gradient that has already faded toward zero. A more structural solution must provide a less distorted route for information and credit.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
7.1 LSTM: retain, write, expose
An LSTM separates the cell state \(\mathbf c_t\) from the visible hidden state \(\mathbf h_t\).

7.1.1 Retain or forget
\[
\mathbf f_t
=\sigma\!\left(W_f[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_f\right).
\]
\(\mathbf f_t\odot\mathbf c_{t-1}\) selects how much previous memory survives.


7.1.2 Prepare a write
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf i_t&=\sigma\!\left(W_i[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_i\right),\\
\mathbf g_t&=\tanh\!\left(W_g[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_g\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\mathbf i_t\) controls write strength; \(\mathbf g_t\) proposes candidate content.


7.1.3 Update memory additively
\[
\mathbf c_t
=\mathbf f_t\odot\mathbf c_{t-1}
+\mathbf i_t\odot\mathbf g_t.
\tag{15}\]
The additive path is the key structural change. When \(\mathbf f_t\) remains near \(1\) and the write term remains small, information and gradient can travel through the cell state with less repeated distortion.


7.1.4 Expose part of memory
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf o_t&=\sigma\!\left(W_o[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_o\right),\\
\mathbf h_t&=\mathbf o_t\odot\tanh(\mathbf c_t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The output gate controls which parts of memory become visible to predictions and the next recurrent step.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
7.2 GRU: reset, propose, interpolate
A GRU combines memory and visible state into one vector. It uses two main gates.

7.2.1 Reset the old state before proposing a candidate
\[
\mathbf r_t
=\sigma\!\left(W_r[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_r\right),
\]
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf h}_t
=\tanh\!\left(W_h[\mathbf r_t\odot\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_h\right).
\]


7.2.2 Interpolate between old and proposed state
\[
\mathbf z_t
=\sigma\!\left(W_z[\mathbf h_{t-1};\mathbf x_t]+\mathbf b_z\right),
\]
\[
\mathbf h_t
=(1-\mathbf z_t)\odot\mathbf h_{t-1}
+\mathbf z_t\odot\widetilde{\mathbf h}_t.
\tag{16}\]
The update is a learned elementwise mixture. A small component of \(\mathbf z_t\) keeps the corresponding old-state component; a large value replaces it with the candidate.



Table 7: Both architectures create learned paths that can preserve information; neither guarantees that every long dependency will be learned.










Property
LSTM
GRU




Persistent representation
cell state \(\mathbf c_t\) plus hidden state \(\mathbf h_t\)
hidden state \(\mathbf h_t\) only


Main controls
forget, input, output
reset, update


State update
additive retain + write
interpolation between old and candidate


Typical advantage
explicit memory highway
simpler gated computation












TipCoding perspective



Libraries expose LSTM and GRU modules because the internal equations are reused at every time step. In implementation, inspect tensor shapes, initial states, returned sequences, and padding masks rather than reimplementing every gate unless the exercise explicitly asks for it.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
8.1 Encoder–decoder recurrence
An encoder reads the source sequence and updates a state:
\[
\mathbf h_t^{\text{enc}}
=f_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf h_{t-1}^{\text{enc}}).
\]
After the final source token, the last encoder state becomes a context vector:
\[
\mathbf c=\mathbf h_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}.
\tag{17}\]
The decoder starts from that context and generates the target sequence:
\[
\mathbf s_t
=f_{\text{dec}}(\mathbf e(y_{t-1}),\mathbf s_{t-1},\mathbf c),
\]
\[
P(y_t\mid y_{<t},\mathbf x)
=\operatorname{softmax}(U\mathbf s_t+\mathbf b).
\]

The source and target may have different lengths. The architecture defines two roles—reading and writing—not a requirement that one parameter matrix perform both roles (Sutskever et al. 2014; Cho et al. 2014).

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
9.1 Training seq2seq end to end
During supervised training, each target token provides a decoder-side cross-entropy loss:
\[
J^{(t)}
=-\log P(y_t\mid y_{<t},\mathbf x).
\]
The sequence loss is
\[
J=\sum_{t=1}^{T_y}J^{(t)}.
\tag{19}\]
No token-level translation loss is attached directly to encoder states. Nevertheless, backpropagation follows the full computation graph:
\[
J
\longrightarrow
\text{decoder states}
\longrightarrow
\mathbf c
\longrightarrow
\text{encoder states and parameters}.
\]
Thus, loss location and update reach are different questions:

losses are computed where target tokens are predicted;
decoder parameters receive direct downstream credit;
the context path receives gradient from the decoder; and
encoder parameters are updated because they produced the context on which every decoder prediction depends.







NoteTeacher forcing



During basic training, the decoder commonly receives the observed previous target token \(y_{t-1}\) rather than its own sampled prediction. This makes all target-side losses computable in parallel across the unrolled training graph, although recurrent states themselves remain sequential. At inference time, the true next tokens are unavailable, so generated tokens must be fed back.

title: Neural Networks for Sequences
text:
10.1 Chapter synthesis
The chapter followed a sequence of architectural repairs:



Table 9: Each repair solves one problem while exposing the next.










Limitation
Repair
Remaining question




exact n-gram counts do not share evidence
embeddings and shared neural parameters
how can context length vary?


fixed neural window grows with position count
recurrent state and weight sharing
how does distant credit survive?


repeated recurrent Jacobians vanish or explode
clipping and gated cells
how should one sequence condition another?


one fixed context summarizes the source
encoder–decoder conditional LM
how can the decoder retrieve specific source information?






An RNN replaces a fixed input window with a learned state. BPTT trains that state across time, but repeated transformations make long-range credit fragile. LSTM and GRU cells create gated, partly additive routes for information. Encoder–decoder models then turn recurrence into a general conditional-generation framework. Their fixed-context bottleneck leaves one question for the next chapter.






ImportantCarry this question forward



Can a decoder retrieve the relevant source information at each output step instead of demanding that one vector remember everything?

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing Chapter 7 · The Transformer architecture
Attention gives a model a powerful communication rule: each token can retrieve a weighted mixture of other representations. A complete Transformer needs more. It must encode order, transform each retrieved message nonlinearly, prevent information leakage during generation, and remain trainable when many blocks are stacked.
This chapter follows the lecture’s construction rather than presenting the final diagram all at once. Each addition repairs one concrete limitation. By the end, the encoder, decoder, and encoder–decoder Transformer will be consequences of a few explicit design choices.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
1.1 The permutation problem
Compare “Alice thanked Bob” with “Bob thanked Alice.” The token identities are the same, but their roles are reversed. Without a separate position signal, self-attention is permutation equivariant. If a permutation matrix \(P\) reorders the rows of \(X\), then
\[
\operatorname{Attn}(PX)=P\operatorname{Attn}(X).
\]
The outputs follow the reordered inputs, but the attention mechanism has no independent fact saying which occurrence came first. This is why the original Transformer adds position representations before the first layer (Vaswani et al. 2017). See also Stanford CS224N Lecture 5 and The Illustrated Transformer.






Figure 2: Without a position signal, self-attention follows a permutation but cannot identify the changed order. This standalone vector figure is generated from the lecture’s original SVG code.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
1.2 Add content and position
For token \(i\), the Transformer input is
\[
\boxed{z_i=e(\text{token}_i)+p_i}.
\tag{1}\]
Both vectors have dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\), so addition preserves one vector per token. The word cats keeps the same lexical embedding wherever it occurs, but adding \(p_1\) or \(p_3\) produces different Transformer inputs.






The positional vector does not replace the token embedding. It perturbs it with an order-dependent signal while preserving the interface expected by attention.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
1.3 Sinusoidal positions
The classical fixed encoding uses paired sine and cosine waves:
\[
\operatorname{PE}(pos,2i)=\sin\!\left(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\right),
\]
\[
\operatorname{PE}(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\left(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\right).
\]
Each feature uses a different wavelength. Nearby positions change smoothly, while the collection of frequencies gives each position a distinctive pattern. The design also makes fixed offsets expressible through linear combinations of sine and cosine terms.






Figure 3: Sinusoidal position encoding: waves at different frequencies, rendered directly from the lecture’s SVG source.



Other approaches include learned absolute embeddings, relative position representations, Transformer-XL relative attention, RoPE, and ALiBi. We focus here on the original sinusoidal construction because it makes the architectural role of position especially clear.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
4.1 Multi-head attention revisited
One head produces one attention distribution per query. Different heads have separate projection matrices and may learn different relations—for example, a subject–verb relation in one head and an entity-reference relation in another:
\[
\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\operatorname{Concat}(head_1,\ldots,head_h)W_O.
\]
This is a capacity argument, not a guarantee that every head receives a clean linguistic interpretation. Clark et al. analyze BERT attention patterns; BertViz provides an interactive inspection tool.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
4.2 Residual connections
A residual sublayer learns a correction to its input:
\[
y=x+F(x).
\]
The identity path carries representations and gradients through depth even when the learned branch is initially unhelpful. The loss-landscape visual used in the lecture comes from Li et al., Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
4.3 Layer normalization
For one token vector \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), LayerNorm computes statistics across its feature dimension:
\[
\mu=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d x_j,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d(x_j-\mu)^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{LN}(x)_j=\gamma_j\frac{x_j-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}+\beta_j.
\tag{4}\]
\(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learned feature-wise parameters. Statistics are computed independently for each token and example—not across tokens in the batch. Consult the original Layer Normalization paper and the torch.nn.LayerNorm documentation.






Figure 5: LayerNorm operates along the feature dimension of each token representation; it does not aggregate across tokens or batches.



class ExplicitLayerNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d_model))
        self.beta = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_model))
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
        return self.gamma * (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + self.eps) + self.beta

layer_norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
The original Transformer uses post-norm sublayers:
\[
\operatorname{LayerNorm}(x+\operatorname{Sublayer}(x)).
\]






Figure 6: The classical post-norm block used in the lecture: each learned sublayer has a residual route followed by Add & Norm.



Many later large models use pre-norm. The distinction matters for optimization, but it does not change the conceptual roles of attention, FFN, residual routing, and normalization.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
5.1 The decoder
A decoder block contains masked multi-head self-attention, Add & Norm, a position-wise FFN, and another Add & Norm. Repeating the block \(L\) times gives
\[
Z^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{DecoderBlock}_{\ell}(Z^{(\ell-1)}).
\]
The final states pass through a vocabulary projection and softmax to produce next-token probabilities. Inputs are shifted target tokens plus position representations.






Figure 7: A decoder is a stack of repeated decoder blocks. Masked self-attention, residual normalization, and the FFN repeat before the final Linear + Softmax head.

title: The Transformer Architecture
section: 5.2 Why the encoder has no causal mask
text:
5.2 Why the encoder has no causal mask
In translation, the complete source sentence is available before generation begins. The decoder must not inspect future French target words, because those are answers it must predict. The encoder, however, should use the complete English sentence: its job is to construct informed source representations.
For “She visited the bank to deposit cash,” the representation of bank benefits from both visited on its left and deposit cash on its right. Thus encoder self-attention uses the full \(T\times T\) score matrix without a triangular causal mask.
An encoder block contains unmasked multi-head self-attention, Add & Norm, a position-wise FFN, and Add & Norm. Repeating it gives
\[
X^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{EncoderBlock}_{\ell}(X^{(\ell-1)}).
\]






Figure 8: The corresponding encoder stack uses the same repeated-block visual language but removes the causal mask, allowing full source context.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
8.1 Translation results
The original Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English→German and 41.8 on English→French. The former improved over the previously reported best systems, including ensembles, by more than two BLEU points. The large model trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs (Vaswani et al. 2017). These results mattered because the architecture combined quality with a much more parallel training computation than recurrence.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
8.2 Transfer across tasks
BERT-Large reported a GLUE score of 80.5, SQuAD 1.1 F1 of 93.2, and SWAG accuracy of 86.3. The important result was not only each number: one pretrained bidirectional encoder could be fine-tuned across many language-understanding tasks. T5 extended this transfer principle by representing every task as text-to-text and reported gains across GLUE, SuperGLUE, question answering, summarization, and translation.






Benchmark metrics are not interchangeable. Compare systems within the same dataset, split, and metric—not a BLEU score directly with an F1 or accuracy score.

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
8.3 Full attention is quadratic
With \(Q,K\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_k}\),
\[
S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}\in\mathbb R^{T\times T}.
\]
There are \(T^2\) query–key scores per head and example, and the classical per-layer attention time is \(\mathcal O(T^2d)\) (Vaswani et al. 2017). Doubling context length quadruples the number of scores:



Context length \(T\)
Scores \(T^2\)




128
16,384


256
65,536


512
262,144


1,024
1,048,576



This limitation motivates sparse attention, linear attention, recurrence or memory, and optimized exact algorithms. Useful entry points include Sparse Transformers, Longformer, Transformers are RNNs, and FlashAttention. These approaches make different trade-offs: some approximate or restrict the attention pattern; FlashAttention computes exact attention while reducing memory traffic.

TipMathematical Foundation



The n-gram probability is calculated as: \[P(w_i|w_{i-n+1}^{i-1}) = \frac{C(w_{i-n+1}^{i})}{C(w_{i-n+1}^{i-1})}\]

Responsible AI development requires comprehensive evaluation and ethical considerations:

Representation Bias: Training data may not represent all populations
Measurement Bias: Evaluation metrics may favor certain groups
Evaluation Bias: Test sets may contain demographic skews

The idea
You will study word embeddings at three increasing levels of difficulty:

Explore: load published GloVe vectors, solve analogies, and visualize semantic groups.

def neighbor_table(vectors, queries: Sequence[str], topn: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for query in queries:
        for rank, (neighbor, similarity) in enumerate(
            vectors.most_similar(query, topn=topn), start=1
        ):
            rows.append(
                {
                    "query": query,
                    "rank": rank,
                    "neighbor": neighbor,
                    "cosine_similarity": similarity,
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def plot_embedding(
    words: Sequence[str],
    points: np.ndarray,
    title: str,
    groups: Sequence[str] | None = None,
):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
    if groups is None:
        groups = ["words"] * len(words)

    group_names = list(dict.fromkeys(groups))
    palette = plt.cm.Set2(np.linspace(0, 1, len(group_names)))
    color_for = dict(zip(group_names, palette))

    for word, (x, y), group in zip(words, points, groups):
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=75, color=color_for[group], label=group)
        ax.annotate(word, (x, y), xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points")

    handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
    unique = dict(zip(labels, handles))
    ax.legend(unique.values(), unique.keys(), frameon=False)
    ax.axhline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Principal component 1")
    ax.set_ylabel("Principal component 2")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

The next function is supplied. It combines every positive pair with three sampled negative pairs and labels them 1 or 0. To keep memory modest, it creates negatives once for this teaching run.

def build_word2vec_dataset(
    centers: torch.Tensor,
    contexts: torch.Tensor,
    negatives_per_positive: int,
) -> TensorDataset:
    negative_centers = centers.repeat_interleave(negatives_per_positive)
    negative_contexts = sample_negative_contexts(len(negative_centers))

    all_centers = torch.cat([centers, negative_centers])
    all_contexts = torch.cat([contexts, negative_contexts])
    labels = torch.cat(
        [torch.ones(len(centers)), torch.zeros(len(negative_centers))]
    )

    order = torch.randperm(len(labels))
    return TensorDataset(all_centers[order], all_contexts[order], labels[order])

Inspect the learned weights
The rows of center_embeddings.weight are the learned vectors. The helper functions below are supplied and will also be reused for GloVe.

def normalized_rows(matrix: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    norms = np.linalg.norm(matrix, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return matrix / np.clip(norms, 1e-12, None)


def nearest_words(
    matrix: np.ndarray,
    query: str,
    word_to_id: dict[str, int],
    id_to_word: dict[int, str],
    topn: int = 5,
):
    if query not in word_to_id:
        return []
    normalized = normalized_rows(matrix)
    query_id = word_to_id[query]
    scores = normalized @ normalized[query_id]
    best = np.argsort(-scores)
    return [
        (id_to_word[index], float(scores[index]))
        for index in best
        if index != query_id
    ][:topn]

print("Weight matrix:", word2vec_weights.shape)

for query in ["king", "queen", "water", "music"]:
    print(query, nearest_words(word2vec_weights, query, word_to_id, id_to_word))

def cooccurrence_dataset(
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], float]

GloVe TODO 3 of 3 · Predict log counts and compute loss
The model parameters are supplied:

a center embedding \(\mathbf{w}_i\);
a context embedding \(\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_j\);
one bias for every center word;
one bias for every context word.

\[

=\mathbf{w}_i^T\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_j+b_i+\widetilde b_j,

then return the mean weighted squared error.

class GloVeModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocabulary_size: int, embedding_dim: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.word_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)
        self.context_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)
        self.word_biases = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, 1)
        self.context_biases = nn.Embedding(vocabulary_size, 1)

        nn.init.normal_(self.word_embeddings.weight, std=0.02)
        nn.init.normal_(self.context_embeddings.weight, std=0.02)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.word_biases.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.context_biases.weight)

    def forward(
        self,
        center_ids: torch.Tensor,
        context_ids: torch.Tensor,
        counts: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        center_vectors = self.word_embeddings(center_ids)
        context_vectors = self.context_embeddings(context_ids)
        center_biases = self.word_biases(center_ids).squeeze(1)
        context_biases = self.context_biases(context_ids).squeeze(1)

        # GLOVE TODO 3: compute predictions, weights, and mean loss.
        # Replace the next line.
        raise NotImplementedError("Return weighted squared error")

The dot product is (center_vectors * context_vectors).sum(dim=1). Add both one-dimensional bias tensors. The result has one prediction per training row.

def train_glove_epoch(model, loader, optimizer) -> float:
    model.train()
    total_loss = 0.0

    for center_ids, context_ids, counts in loader:
        center_ids = center_ids.to(DEVICE)
        context_ids = context_ids.to(DEVICE)
        counts = counts.to(DEVICE)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = model(center_ids, context_ids, counts)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        total_loss += loss.item() * len(counts)

    return total_loss / len(loader.dataset)

title: How Do Words Learn Meaning?
section: Why learn biases as well as vectors?
text:
Why learn biases as well as vectors?



Broad frequency effects

In our ledger, water has 20 total context occurrences; solid has 10.
A context bias can capture a broadly higher baseline without making every vector point toward water.



Specific compatibility

solid occurs 8 times near ice but 2 near steam.
One shared solid bias cannot explain that contrast alone. The vector interactions must capture the remaining structure.



\[\underbrace{\mathbf w_i^T\widetilde{\mathbf w}_j}_{\text{pair interaction}}
+\underbrace{b_i+\widetilde b_j}_{\text{word-specific baselines}}
\;\approx\;\log X_{ij}\]


Biases are learned offsets, not fixed word counts. The model shares them across a row or column.

title: How Do Words Learn Meaning?

text:
Count 1 and count 1,000 should not vote equally

Use a reliability weight: rise for small positive counts, then cap the influence of frequent pairs.




Teaching setting: xmax = 10


X = 10.178


X = 20.299


X = 80.846


X ≥ 101.000



\[f(x)=\min\left((x/10)^{3/4},1\right),\quad x>0\]
For our ice → solid cell:
\[f(8)\,e^2\approx0.846\times0.144\approx\mathbf{0.122}\]
The paper uses \(x_{max}=100\) in its reported experiments; 10 is our toy setting.



Train on nonzero cells. A zero is omitted; GloVe never evaluates \(\log 0\) or treats it as a negative-sampling example.

section: Why can this recover the ratio idea?
text:
Why can this recover the ratio idea?

Return to the same two rows and the same probe solid. Subtract their fitted log counts.


\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf w_{ice}^{T}\widetilde{\mathbf w}_{solid}+b_{ice}+\widetilde b_{solid}&\approx\log 8\\
\mathbf w_{steam}^{T}\widetilde{\mathbf w}_{solid}+b_{steam}+\widetilde b_{solid}&\approx\log 2
\end{aligned}\]

↓ subtract · the context bias cancels

\[(\mathbf w_{ice}-\mathbf w_{steam})^T\widetilde{\mathbf w}_{solid}
+(b_{ice}-b_{steam})\approx\log 4\]


The same vector difference is tested against solid, gas, and water. Each probe exposes a different part of the relationship.


The center-bias difference remains; do not imply it cancels. Here the two row totals are equal, so count ratios equal conditional-probability ratios. With unequal totals, log probability ratios also subtract the log row-total ratio; this motivates row offsets. The ratio idea motivates the model, but training fits weighted log counts, not explicit ratio labels.

    From Large to Small Models: How Much Knowledge Can Be Transferred?
    BEN SBEH Chaimae · CHAOU Nabila · CHAKKOUR Karima
    
      Project description
      This project investigates whether knowledge distillation can improve small models for banking intent classification. Using the Banking77 benchmark, we will transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. We aim to understand how student size and the amount of labeled training data influence the effectiveness of distillation.

    Knowing When Not to Answer: Abstention in Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering
    Youssef Ech-chahlaoui · Zouhair Fezzaz
    
      Project description
      This project investigates whether a retrieval-augmented question-answering system can recognize when its retrieved evidence does not support an answer. We will compare a standard answer-generating baseline with lightweight abstention strategies based on retrieval scores and answerability signals, using answerable and unanswerable questions. We aim to identify when these strategies improve reliability and when they incorrectly refuse valid questions.
    
  



  
    
    
  
  
    Does Reranking Fix 'Lost in the Middle'? Cross-Encoder Reranking in Small-LLM RAG, in English and French
    Yasmine El Alaoui · Fatima Zahrae Ahannuk · Merouane Ayach
    
      Project description
      We study whether cross-encoder reranking reduces the "Lost in the Middle" effect when small open-source LLMs answer questions over a niche video-game wiki. We compare vanilla retrieval-augmented generation with a reranked pipeline, vary where the key evidence sits in the prompt, and test two models with questions in English and French, measuring accuracy and latency.

    Local Personal Data Masking Before Sharing Documents with LLMs
    Konate Bachirou · Sylla Karamo
    
      Project description
      Sharing documents with external LLMs can expose personal information. We will build a system that processes French documents locally, detects personal data using fine-tuned CamemBERT, and replaces it with descriptive labels before sharing. Users will be able to review the masked text. We will evaluate detection accuracy, masking errors, and CPU performance to assess the system's usefulness and limitations.
    
  



  
    
    Original AI-assisted illustration by the team
  
  
    When Does Neural Memory Fail? Investigating Distractors in Multi-Hop Reasoning
    Bjibji Hamza · Elbouk Abderrahimane
    
      Project description
      Can neural networks retrieve relevant information when surrounded by distracting facts? We propose implementing an End-to-End Memory Network from scratch, based on the 2015 research paper. Using the bAbI question-answering dataset, we will compare memory-hop configurations and investigate how irrelevant sentences affect performance to better understand attention-based memory in multi-fact reasoning.
    
  



  
    
    
  
  
    How Can We Perform Sentiment Analysis on Amazon Food Reviews?
    Michel Sagesse KOLIE
    
      Project description
      This project studies sentiment in Amazon Food Reviews and explores how different NLP methods interpret customer opinions. We will compare VADER, RoBERTa, BERT-based embeddings and fine-tuning, and single- and two-layer LSTM models for negative, neutral and positive classification. We will also build a retrieval-augmented generation system to explore review evidence and summarize customer feedback.
    
  



  
    
    AI-generated illustration created by the team for this proposal.

    Ismail Rachidi · Haytham El Harraq
    
      Project description
      Football supporters often ask the same question in different words or languages. We will build a small tool that flags likely duplicate questions in a football FAQ. We will compare word overlap with a multilingual sentence model and test whether cross-language pairs are harder than same-language pairs. We will inspect errors before claiming the tool is useful.

      Moroccan Darija is frequently written using Latin characters and digits (Arabizi), creating challenges for automatic text processing. title: Student Projects
text:
What makes a good project?
A strong project can take either of two directions: a deep implementation from scratch of a model from the research literature, or a thoughtful application of an existing model to a real problem. Both are equally valid. Choose the direction that lets you demonstrate understanding, make meaningful decisions, and support your conclusions with evidence.

Direction 1 · Understand a model by building it
Choose a published model and implement its central mechanisms yourself. Explain how the paper’s ideas become code, verify that the implementation behaves as intended, and investigate at least one design choice through a controlled experiment. You may use PyTorch and automatic differentiation; identify clearly which components you implement and which you reuse. A smaller model and dataset are acceptable when they let you study the mechanism carefully.

Word2Vec from scratch: Implement skip-gram with negative sampling, train on a manageable corpus, and investigate how context-window size changes the learned word relationships.
An attention-based translation model: Build an encoder–decoder with attention, trace how it uses the source sentence, and compare it with a version without attention on the same translation task.
A miniature Transformer language model: Implement causal self-attention, positional information, and Transformer blocks, then examine how context length affects predictions and generation errors.



Direction 2 · Use a model to solve a real problem
Choose a concrete user need and apply or adapt an existing model using relevant data. The contribution lies in the complete investigation: preparing the data, choosing an approach, comparing it with a simple baseline, evaluating realistic cases, and explaining failures. Show what the system helps a user accomplish and where it still needs improvement.

A university regulations assistant: Build a question-answering system over actual university documents that cites its sources, then evaluate answer correctness and its behavior when the documents do not contain an answer.
Routing multilingual support requests: Adapt an existing classifier to assign French, Arabic, or Darija requests to the right service, and inspect which categories and language mixtures cause routing errors.
Extracting information from local job advertisements: Use an existing language model to extract skills, experience requirements, and locations, then evaluate the extracted fields against manually checked examples for a searchable job catalogue.

For either direction, state one clear question, compare against a baseline, and discuss concrete errors. The project’s strength comes from the depth of the implementation or the usefulness of the application, supported by careful evaluation. These examples are starting points; you may propose your own topic.

text:

01Learning from raw textA large corpus supplies its own targets. Where do unfamiliar spellings fit?


02The BERT ideaHide or replace tokens; recover the original using context.


03Three families, three recipesEncoder, decoder, encoder–decoder: inputs, targets, losses, and uses.


04Pretrain once, adapt to tasksFine-tune BERT for sentiment, sentence pairs, and question answering.


05What did the model learn?Probe context, knowledge, and typo robustness; check for memorization.


06Modern pretraining at scaleData and compute choices in Llama 3; open training with OLMo.



A model can learn to predict text. What else must it learn to follow an instruction?


Reading path: Stanford CS224N · Pretraining · BERT · T5 · Llama 3 · Olmo 3


The instructor’s revised sequence starts with learning from a large unlabeled corpus, develops BERT’s contextual recovery task, compares the three Transformer families and their training recipes, then shows transfer through simple task heads and supervised fine-tuning. The two concluding sections examine learned capabilities and limitations, then modern data/compute choices. The reference PDF’s filename says lecture07; its title page says Lecture 6: Pretraining.
Keep the distinction precise: subword/byte representations help encode unfamiliar spellings; BERT’s deliberate token corruption supplies self-supervised targets. Neither implies guaranteed understanding of misspellings. In original BERT, select 15% of token positions; of those selected positions, use MASK 80%, random replacement 10%, and unchanged input 10%. Predict the original token at all selected positions. Mention original next-sentence prediction as a historical second objective, not a requirement for every encoder.
For the three families, retain one sentence and show visible context, target alignment, scored positions, and one training update: BERT masked-token prediction, GPT causal next-token prediction, and T5 corrupted-span reconstruction with a causal decoder. Architecture and objective are related choices, not exclusive lists of permitted downstream tasks. Do not reteach the Transformer blocks from Lecture 07.
For transfer, contrast pretraining’s automatically obtained targets with task labels. Show a sentiment head, a sentence-pair head, and extractive QA start/end heads. Fine-tuning normally updates the pretrained backbone as well as the task head. Compare pretrained and randomly initialized versions under the same downstream budget. Historical BERT results must be labeled as such, not current rankings.
The final sections should use controlled context/typo interventions, fixed-input checkpoint comparisons, and research evidence on data quality, data mixtures, and training budgets. Llama 3 is the intended “Herd of Models” reference; Olmo 3 supplies an open model-flow case study. Briefly distinguish in-context examples (fixed weights) from fine-tuning (updated weights). Keep instruction tuning, preference optimization, and efficient adaptation for Lecture 09. The detailed authoring plan and references are in OUTLINE.md. Sections 1–4 follow; stop at the Section 4 bridge for instructor review.

Begin with the encoder’s middle square. Trace all three incoming lines to the lower row: it can use left, self, and right context. Repeat in the next layer. Here x is any supplied source (including corrupted text for T5 pretraining); the following recipe slide gives exact sentinels and reconstruction targets. The tokenizer stays fixed. The word embeddings and contextual layers are loaded from a pretrained checkpoint. Each new downstream task ordinarily starts from its own copy of that checkpoint and adds its own head; this is not sequentially overwriting one model with three tasks. Trace bottom to top. The visible token strings are a teaching sequence, not a claim about exact production tokenization. Embeddings enter bidirectional Transformer layers. All supplied tokens can affect the final CLS vector. The diagram shows one representative mixing stage, not BERT’s full depth. The highlighted lines focus on CLS, but all other contextual states are also computed. CLS is a learned input symbol at position zero; its final representation is context-dependent, not a fixed sentence embedding and not an arithmetic mean. Supervised training makes the classifier use this state for sentiment.
W and b are newly initialized task parameters. For two classes, W has two rows and as many columns as the hidden-state dimension; b has two entries. The vector z contains scores, not probabilities. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities over the two classes. We use a direct linear head on final CLS for this lesson and the recorded comparison; implementations may use a pretrained pooler or dropout before the head. A pretrained encoder with a random sentiment head is not already a trained sentiment classifier. No measured sentiment probabilities are shown here.

Bring back the last slide of Section 4. Students have seen the model’s aggregate held-out accuracy, but this hides which distinctions it makes. Ask them for the intended labels before showing the next slide. Here “lovde” is an authored typo for “loved,” not a newly defined word. Fixing the weights means that any change in the output comes from the changed input and its tokenization, not further training. We also keep the tokenizer, inference settings and decision rule fixed.
These are behavioral diagnostics: we observe outputs under controlled changes. A representation probe is a different experiment: train a separate predictor to recover an annotation, such as a part-of-speech tag, from saved hidden vectors. Successful recovery would show accessible information, but would not by itself prove that the original model uses that information for its task. We focus on behavior here because students can inspect the input and output directly. A single failure can refute a universal claim; a few successes cannot establish one. Larger, systematically constructed test sets are needed.

The two boxes are conceptual examples, not records from the paper. In the published study, researchers generated 600,000 samples, selected candidates with extraction strategies, and verified training matches. The 604 verified cases establish that extraction occurred; their proportion among inspected candidates is not an estimate of memorization frequency for ordinary use. Correctness on novel examples and verbatim reproduction are compatible behaviors of one model. Recall of a common fact alone is not evidence of passage memorization.

Walk left to right. The test question is reserved when constructing the small labeled fine-tuning set, but it already influenced the weights in an earlier stage. This breaks the intended interpretation of “unseen.” It need not involve intentional cheating or an explicit answer column; passages that reveal the answer can also overlap. Deduplicating fine-tuning against evaluation is useful, but is narrower than auditing the pretraining corpus. Exact-match checks miss paraphrases and related documents. Document-level or source-level splits and genuinely later data can strengthen the design when their assumptions hold.
For our classroom experiment, exact normalized overlaps were removed between the sampled SST-2 training and validation texts. We do not have sufficient evidence to certify the validation examples absent from the model’s complete historical pretraining. State that limit rather than treating the held-out accuracy as proof of exposure-free generalization. Avoid identifying a particular wrong or right response as memorization from its score alone.

Our route through pretraining


01Learning from raw textA large corpus supplies its own targets. Where do unfamiliar spellings fit?


02The BERT ideaHide or replace tokens; recover the original using context.


03Three families, three recipesEncoder, decoder, encoder–decoder: inputs, targets, losses, and uses.

A model can learn to predict text. What else must it learn to follow an instruction?


Reading path: Stanford CS224N · Pretraining · BERT · T5 · Llama 3 · Olmo 3


The instructor’s revised sequence starts with learning from a large unlabeled corpus, develops BERT’s contextual recovery task, compares the three Transformer families and their training recipes, then shows transfer through simple task heads and supervised fine-tuning. The two concluding sections examine learned capabilities and limitations, then modern data/compute choices. The reference PDF’s filename says lecture07; its title page says Lecture 6: Pretraining.
Keep the distinction precise: subword/byte representations help encode unfamiliar spellings; BERT’s deliberate token corruption supplies self-supervised targets. Neither implies guaranteed understanding of misspellings. In original BERT, select 15% of token positions; of those selected positions, use MASK 80%, random replacement 10%, and unchanged input 10%. Predict the original token at all selected positions. Mention original next-sentence prediction as a historical second objective, not a requirement for every encoder.
For the three families, retain one sentence and show visible context, target alignment, scored positions, and one training update: BERT masked-token prediction, GPT causal next-token prediction, and T5 corrupted-span reconstruction with a causal decoder. Architecture and objective are related choices, not exclusive lists of permitted downstream tasks. Do not reteach the Transformer blocks from Lecture 07.
For transfer, contrast pretraining’s automatically obtained targets with task labels. Show a sentiment head, a sentence-pair head, and extractive QA start/end heads. Fine-tuning normally updates the pretrained backbone as well as the task head. Compare pretrained and randomly initialized versions under the same downstream budget. Historical BERT results must be labeled as such, not current rankings.
The final sections should use controlled context/typo interventions, fixed-input checkpoint comparisons, and research evidence on data quality, data mixtures, and training budgets. Llama 3 is the intended “Herd of Models” reference; Olmo 3 supplies an open model-flow case study. Briefly distinguish in-context examples (fixed weights) from fine-tuning (updated weights). Keep instruction tuning, preference optimization, and efficient adaptation for Lecture 09. The detailed authoring plan and references are in OUTLINE.md. Mean cross-entropy over selected positions · one training example shown; training averages over examples and corruption draws. Gradients update the prediction head and contextual reader.


The cat term is twice the mat term here. Keep the example visible while mapping to x, corrupted x, and M. M includes every selected position, even when its input is a random token or unchanged. The normalization shown is our per-example mean convention; batching can average over all selected tokens. The MLM head produces vocabulary logits from contextual states, and softmax converts them into the probabilities used here. Backpropagation connects these errors to the head, Transformer layers, and embeddings. This is a sum of token prediction losses conditioned on the same corrupted sequence, not a left-to-right factorization of the probability of the complete sentence. No additional hand labels were supplied.

Original drawing using the visual convention of Raffel et al., T5, Fig. 4, p. 17 and Stanford CS224N. Connections show permission, not measured weights. Feed-forward, residual and normalization operations omitted.


This is a token-state architecture drawing, not a pipeline of opaque labeled boxes. Read bottom to top. Every square represents a vector at a sequence position, not a neuron or an entire layer. The same colored row belongs to one stage of a Transformer stack. Edges show allowed attention dependencies across stages, not the numerical attention weights. Fully visible does not mean all positions receive equal weight. Line colors and shapes distinguish full, causal, and cross-attention connections.
Begin with the encoder’s middle square. Trace all three incoming lines to the lower row: it can use left, self, and right context. Repeat in the next layer. Its supplied input is “the [M] sat”; the original masked word is not available along any path. Top h1/h2/h3 are contextual states, not predicted words. A vocabulary head for masked-token recovery will appear in the recipe slide.
Move to the decoder-only middle square. It has only two incoming lines: from the first and second positions. The rightmost lower state has no path to it. This restriction repeats at every layer. Read the bottom input “start, the, cat” against the top next-token targets “the, cat, sat”. The current input token may be read because the prediction target is shifted. Thin coral arrows at the top abbreviate a vocabulary prediction head. Targets are labels/prediction positions, not guaranteed model outputs. All positions can be computed together during teacher-forced training.
The encoder–decoder panel separates source and target streams. Source x1/x2/x3 pass through fully visible encoder layers on the left. The decoder receives “start, y1” at the bottom right and produces distributions for y1/y2 at the top. First trace the causal self-attention connections. Then trace the dashed coral connections from all final encoder states into each decoder position: these are cross-attention. The vertical target-stream lines carry the decoder’s own state into that cross-attention stage; they do not indicate target self-attention becoming bidirectional. Decoder queries attend to encoder keys and values. Cross-attention occurs in each actual decoder block; only one such block’s two attention stages are expanded here. The encoder drawing shows two illustrative layers and the decoder shows two distinct attention sublayers, so row counts are not a depth comparison.
The T5 paper’s Figure 4 compares encoder–decoder, causal language model, and prefix language model. We borrow its token-state drawing convention but retain our lecture’s encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder–decoder categories. Do not call the paper’s prefix LM an encoder-only model. Here x is any supplied source (including corrupted text for T5 pretraining); the following recipe slide gives exact sentinels and reconstruction targets. The encoder and decoder-only panels use tiny word examples to make the attention permissions inspectable; the third uses x/y to distinguish the two sequences. Ask students to predict the direction before revealing the result. This tests a particular initialization choice under a fixed small downstream budget, not whether pretraining always wins. BERT-tiny is the same architecture family used earlier in the lecture, not BERT-base. A fresh direct linear head on final CLS is initialized identically within each seed pair. Both branches have exactly the same architecture, tokenizer, parameter count, dropout policy, optimizer, minibatches and training steps. Only encoder initialization changes. The model’s pooler is omitted in both branches.
We use class-balanced samples drawn deterministically: 128 training examples per class and 64 original validation examples per class. Exact normalized text overlaps with the selected validation set are removed from the training pool before sampling. This does not rule out related phrases or original pretraining overlap. Original validation labels are held out from updates and no hyperparameters or checkpoint were selected on these results. The experiment uses one learning rate and one budget rather than separately tuning each branch. At 80 steps, 1,280 minibatch examples have been processed, reusing the same 256 labels over five passes. Three seeds are not enough for a broad significance claim. A diagnostic asks a narrow question. One success does not establish general understanding.

Bring back the last slide of Section 4. Students have seen the model’s aggregate held-out accuracy, but this hides which distinctions it makes. Ask them for the intended labels before showing the next slide. Here “lovde” is an authored typo for “loved,” not a newly defined word. Fixing the weights means that any change in the output comes from the changed input and its tokenization, not further training. We also keep the tokenizer, inference settings and decision rule fixed.
These are behavioral diagnostics: we observe outputs under controlled changes. A representation probe is a different experiment: train a separate predictor to recover an annotation, such as a part-of-speech tag, from saved hidden vectors. Successful recovery would show accessible information, but would not by itself prove that the original model uses that information for its task. We focus on behavior here because students can inspect the input and output directly. A single failure can refute a universal claim; a few successes cannot establish one. Larger, systematically constructed test sets are needed.

Good average test performance does not rule out reproducing particular training examples.
Carlini et al., Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models, §6.2 · selected candidates, not a random sample of ordinary queries.

The two boxes are conceptual examples, not records from the paper. In the published study, researchers generated 600,000 samples, selected candidates with extraction strategies, and verified training matches. The 604 verified cases establish that extraction occurred; their proportion among inspected candidates is not an estimate of memorization frequency for ordinary use. Correctness on novel examples and verbatim reproduction are compatible behaviors of one model. Recall of a common fact alone is not evidence of passage memorization.

text:
Held out from which stage?
A test question can be absent from fine-tuning and still appear in pretraining.

A clean fine-tuning split alone cannot establish that evaluation content is unseen.
Schematic contamination example, not a claim that our SST-2 items occurred in BERT-tiny pretraining.

Walk left to right. The test question is reserved when constructing the small labeled fine-tuning set, but it already influenced the weights in an earlier stage. This breaks the intended interpretation of “unseen.” It need not involve intentional cheating or an explicit answer column; passages that reveal the answer can also overlap. Deduplicating fine-tuning against evaluation is useful, but is narrower than auditing the pretraining corpus. Exact-match checks miss paraphrases and related documents. Document-level or source-level splits and genuinely later data can strengthen the design when their assumptions hold.
For our classroom experiment, exact normalized overlaps were removed between the sampled SST-2 training and validation texts. We do not have sufficient evidence to certify the validation examples absent from the model’s complete historical pretraining. State that limit rather than treating the held-out accuracy as proof of exposure-free generalization. Avoid identifying a particular wrong or right response as memorization from its score alone.

Summarize the epistemic lesson: report the observation first and scope the inference to the experiment. Our small model responds to context but fails some simple tests; published studies show why robustness, training membership and social associations need separate evaluations. TIME: 2 minutes. Begin with the sentence, not a definition of pretraining. Ask: “What should the sentiment label be?” Then trace input, Transformer, head, output. The question mark is deliberate: a newly initialized model has no reason to produce the desired label. Positive is the supplied annotation, not its output.
Connect to Lecture 07: the architecture specifies a computation; the numerical parameters still need learning. In this from-scratch setup, the embedding table, contextual layers, and task head all start untrained. The small graph inside the box is symbolic, not a Transformer layer diagram or measured attention.
Reveal the final statement. A modest labeled dataset must provide evidence for both language-sensitive features and the task decision. This is not a proof that training from scratch never works; it motivates a reusable starting point. Transition: “We already know one way to borrow something learned from text: pretrained word embeddings. What do they give us, and what is still missing?”

TIME: 3 minutes. Brief retrieval of Word2Vec: it learned a table of word vectors from prediction tasks constructed from text. Do not reteach skip-gram or its loss. Read the two sentences and ask students to identify the two senses of bank. Point to the single lookup row: the word type selects the same parameters in both contexts. The six colored cells are a visual symbol for a vector, not a six-dimensional Word2Vec measurement or interpretable semantic axes.
Important distinction: a model USING static embeddings can still distinguish the two meanings through its later contextual layers. We are locating what the lookup itself does, not claiming that Word2Vec-based systems cannot use context. The surrounding network still has to learn how to interpret these vectors in sentences. This follows Berkeley’s Word2Vec limitation discussion and Stanford’s contextual-meaning motivation. Transition: “Could the representation we reuse already depend on the sentence?”

TIME: 2 minutes. Switch between money and river while students watch the word lookup and output. The word and model parameters are fixed; the surrounding tokens change. The left vector remains identical; the right symbol changes. This is an explanatory interaction, not inference. Do not describe its chosen colors as experimental evidence that a model distinguishes senses.
The final state at a token position depends on the contextual computation. Write or read h(bank | sentence) as “the representation of bank in this sentence.” Contextual does not itself mean pretrained: an untrained contextual network can also produce different outputs. Pretraining aims to make the representations USEFUL. To test meaning, we would compare actual representations or downstream behavior across many examples; no cosine calculation is needed here.
The discussion adapts Berkeley p.8’s play-in-different-contexts exercise. Ask for the expected financial-context match, then distinguish that expectation from a measurement. Transition: “ELMo made this idea concrete: contextual representations could be learned in advance and then supplied to another task model.” The next slide defines the name and gives a brief empirical example.

section: Give the whole model a head start
text:
Give the whole model a head start

WHAT IS ALREADY LEARNED BEFORE THE TASK?


EARLIER STARTING POINTPretrained word embeddingsThe contextual layers still start from random weights.
WHOLE-MODEL PRETRAININGPretrained contextual layers tooThe task starts from a model already trained on text.

Figures reproduced from Diyi Yang, Stanford CS224N (2026), pretraining lecture, PDF pp. 10–11. Original colors retained; these are schematic networks.


TIME: 3 minutes. Use the real source drawings as the central evidence of the conceptual change. First explain the color key. Trace the red lookup row into the gray contextual layers on the left, then repeat the trace on the right. The difference is which parameter groups have a pretrained initialization. Neither drawing says those weights must remain frozen during task training.
Stanford’s drawing is deliberately generic and shows a prediction roof. Do not infer that a downstream sentiment head is already trained: the pretraining head may be replaced, and the new task head can start randomly initialized. The original roof is not a promise that a pretrained checkpoint solves any task.
Distinguish parameters from representations: parameters are saved and reused; contextual output vectors are computed afresh for each input. The network can reuse patterns learned across a large corpus, then adapt to the new task. This is an initialization strategy, not a claim of guaranteed performance gains. Transition: “Let’s follow those learned parameter values through the two stages.”

title: Pretraining Language Models
section: Pretrain once. Adapt to a new task.
text:
Pretrain once. Adapt to a new task.
RAW TEXT→LEARN PARAMETERS θ→SAVE WEIGHTS→INITIALIZE THE TASK MODEL


copy θ→parameter values


Add the task head; continue learning from labeled reviews.
Reusable word vectors→Contextual representations→A reusable model
Reviews come with sentiment labels.If pretraining data is just text, where do the answers come from?

Figures: Stanford CS224N, PDF p. 19 (printed slide 20). Transfer motivation: Berkeley CS288, pp. 19–20. Arrows and staged annotations added for this course.


TIME: 4 minutes including synthesis. The Stanford figure introduces two stages; its internal text already previews language modeling. Point at the observed text and say that prediction targets will be constructed from it in the next section. Do not yet derive shifting, masking, or a loss. The complete workflow comes first.
Initially show pretraining and the save-weights step. On the first advance, reveal the parameter-copy arrow and task stage together. What crosses the arrow is a set of numerical weights, not the corpus and not a table of cached sentence vectors. We initialize the reusable backbone from those values, attach the task head as needed, and train on labeled examples. The shown sentiment symbol is the task output interface, not a measured result for a specific review.
Full fine-tuning ordinarily updates both backbone and head. Pretrained does not mean frozen, and pretraining is not repeated from scratch for every new task. Each task can begin from its own copy of the checkpoint. Details of heads and freezing belong to Session 2. The simplified diagram does not distinguish which original pretraining heads are discarded; explain this verbally if asked.
On the second advance, synthesize the progression: word vectors, contextual representations, reusable model parameters. Then expose the missing ingredient: we can point to a sentiment annotation, but the raw corpus has no such annotation column. Ask where the training answers could come from. Allow students to propose ideas, then stop at this bridge. The next section constructs self-supervised examples; it has not been authored in this review increment.

title: Pretraining Language Models
section: ELMo: contextual features we can reuse
text:
ELMo: contextual features we can reuse

Embeddings from Language Models · Peters et al., 2018



A word representation built from the internal states of pretrained forward and backward LSTM language models.
left context →word← right context
Mix their layer representations to give each word a vector that depends on its sentence.
Reuse as features: keep the language-model weights fixed while training the task model and the layer mixture.


Do pretrained features help with fewer labels?

Horizontal: fraction of labeled task-training data.Vertical: SNLI accuracy / SRL F1 (higher is better).
Larger gains when task labels are scarce.


The language model supplies features.The downstream model still learns its own task.

Peters et al. (2018), Deep Contextualized Word Representations, §§3.1–3.3, 5.4 and Figure 1 (PDF p. 8). Original published curves, not classroom runs. SNLI: sentence-pair inference; SRL: semantic role labeling.


TIME: 1 minute, taken from the preceding context comparison; the section remains 15 minutes. Expand ELMo aloud: Embeddings from Language Models. It uses LSTMs, not Transformers. The forward model uses preceding words and the backward model uses following words. Their hidden states and the context-independent token representation are mixed with learned task-specific weights. The diagram is a conceptual summary; it is not a bidirectional prediction model allowed to see the answer during language-model pretraining.
Explain the feature-based setup in one sentence: hold the pretrained language model fixed while learning how to combine its representations and how to solve the downstream task. The paper also describes optional domain adaptation of the language model before downstream use; “fixed” here refers to supervised task training in §3.3, not a ban on every possible later language-model update.
Read Figure 1: x is the percentage of the labeled task training set, on a log scale. It does not mean that the language model was pretrained on only 0.1% of its corpus. Left: SNLI sentence-pair inference accuracy. Right: semantic role labeling F1, identifying who did what to whom. These are different metrics, so do not compare their absolute heights across panels. Solid is with ELMo, dashed is the task baseline. Both curves improve as task data increases; ELMo’s advantage is larger in the smaller-data conditions. The paper discusses these experiments in §5.4; the figure itself does not label the evaluation split, so do not invent a test/dev designation. No confidence intervals are shown.
This supports the value of contextual features for these tasks and settings, not a guarantee for every model or dataset. Keep the plot discussion brief; no loss, mixture-weight equation, or benchmark survey is needed. Transition: “ELMo reuses contextual features. The next step is to reuse the contextual model itself as the starting point for task-specific training.”

title: Pretraining Language Models
section: The answer is already in the text
text:
The answer is already in the text

title: Pretraining Language Models
section: Our missing-word task becomes masked language modeling
text:
Our missing-word task becomes masked language modeling

Our example: the [MASK] sat on the mat → target: cat


Now trace the same mechanism in Berkeley’s two-target example.



Architecture: read both sides of the supplied input.Objective: recover original tokens at selected positions.


Diagram cropped from Berkeley CS288, Spring 2026, PDF p. 36; BERT: Devlin et al. (2019), §3.1. Target labels are not measured predictions. Two masks illustrate the mechanism, not a literal 15% rate.


TIME: 2 minutes. Continue directly from the approved architecture bridge. We have already built input–target pairs; BERT gives us a concrete training recipe for an encoder. Lowercase the running sentence and omit its punctuation throughout this section to keep token positions stable. This is a teaching convention, not a claim that all BERT tokenizers lowercase text.
Read Berkeley’s diagram bottom to top. The supplied input has two replacements. The encoder builds a contextual state at every position. A shared vocabulary head uses selected states to assign probabilities to the original tokens. The labels capital and Sacramento above the encoder identify the observed targets, not successful model predictions. The pink Loss labels identify comparison points; they are not extra input to the encoder. Our cat example uses the same mechanism.
Do not repeat softmax arithmetic. Explain that seeing both sides means seeing both sides of the CORRUPTED input. It does not grant access to the original hidden word. This diagram shows only the mask branch; selected positions can also be randomly replaced or unchanged. We will inspect those cases shortly. Transition: “What exactly goes into each encoder position?”

Original example-based drawing following Devlin et al., Fig. 2; Stanford CS224N, PDF pp. 27–28. Each colored box denotes a vector, not a scalar.


TIME: 4 minutes. Tokenization was taught earlier; do not reteach its algorithm. Words can split into WordPieces. Here the short lowercase words are displayed as individual token positions; punctuation is omitted. Position 0 is CLS, cat was at position 2, and SEP ends this single segment at position 7. Trace position 2: E([MASK]) + P2 + S(A) forms the input vector. The three vectors have the same dimension and are added coordinate by coordinate, not concatenated. BERT learns the embedding tables, including the position table. The original cat embedding is not secretly inserted at this masked position. Normalization, dropout, and the internal Transformer operations are omitted from the drawing.
Every final h is contextual. The MLM head reads h2 to predict cat. CLS is a learned special token whose final contextual state can feed a sequence-level head; it is not an arithmetic average of token states. SEP marks a separator/end boundary, not a target word in our MLM selection. Padding, if used in a batch, is excluded from selection and hidden with an attention mask. That padding mask is different from replacing a word by the literal MASK token.
Ask students which vector differs between the two occurrences of the: position embeddings differ even though the token lookup is shared. No numeric vector values are claimed. Transition: “Which positions should become prediction targets?”

First decide which WordPiece positions are selected. Then, separately for each selected position, choose mask/random/unchanged. Selection and corruption are performed while preparing training examples; they are not model predictions. The training procedure retains the original token ID before changing the input.
Do not introduce a second arithmetic exercise or ask students to calculate population percentages here. The next slide inspects one selected position. Original diagrams adapted from Berkeley CS288, PDF pp. 43–46, and BERT Fig. 1. Illustrative target labels; O = outside a named entity. Word-level alignment shown; subword alignment deferred.


TIME: 3 minutes. This is a preview of usefulness, not the detailed adaptation section reserved for Session 2. Read both diagrams bottom to top. On the left, the final CLS state feeds a classifier with task labels such as positive/negative. On the right, a shared classifier reads each token state and predicts its entity label. The shown words stand in for aligned token states; actual subword handling requires an explicit labeling convention. O means outside an entity. Special tokens receive no entity labels in this illustration.
The outputs are authored target labels, not measured model predictions. Neither head arrives trained for these tasks merely because MLM pretraining finished. Each task uses its own model copy initialized from the same pretrained backbone. Task training normally uses complete text rather than artificial MLM masks. Full fine-tuning updates the backbone and the newly attached head together; using frozen features is another possibility we will compare in Session 2.
Keep this focused on the interface: a sequence state versus per-token states. The expensive reusable object is the learned parameter set, not a cache of the specific cat sentence’s vectors. Ask which head the personal-data masking student project resembles. Transition: “This gives us a reader. What if we need to continue text when the words on the right do not exist yet?”

Conceptual information flow, not measured attention. Next: GPT and causal prediction. BERT-style encoders can support other generation procedures; the original MLM recipe is not a left-to-right generation recipe.


TIME: 2 minutes. Synthesize BERT before raising the next question. It reads the supplied corrupted sequence, learns original selected tokens, and yields weights we can reuse. Recall that random and unchanged selected positions also belong to its loss set. The NSP objective was an additional part of the original recipe.
Trace the moving dashed paths: they show allowed information flowing into a prediction, not learned attention magnitudes or a running model. The upper gap has words on both sides already available. The lower prefix has no existing right context. We cannot reveal future words during a task meant to predict them from the past. Do not introduce GPT’s shifted target equation or causal factorization here; leave that mechanism for the next reviewed section.
Avoid the absolute claim that BERT cannot generate text. The limitation motivating our next recipe is that masked reconstruction does not directly train the ordinary left-to-right continuation procedure. End with the displayed question and stop.

GPT: use language modeling to learn reusable weights

The autoregressive objective is familiar. Its role here is to prepare a model for reuse.

Transfer the learned parameters, together with the model’s tokenizer and configuration.


The corpus supplies the supervision. Corpus selection and preprocessing shape what the model can learn.


Original teaching diagram. Berkeley CS288, PDF pp. 57–59; Radford et al. (2018), §3. Authored corpus excerpts; no training run is shown.


TIME: 3 minutes. The instructor explicitly confirmed that prediction, causal attention, and AR generation have already been taught. Do not rederive them. The new point is the role of the learning stage: train on general text, then reuse its weights rather than initialize every downstream model from scratch.
Trace the three passages into training windows. These are authored illustrations, not a sample of a measured training corpus. Actual windows can contain multiple sentences and are bounded by the model’s context length; segmentation, document boundaries, tokenization, filtering, and deduplication are data decisions. We will study data and scale in Session 2. Corpus size alone does not define pretraining.
The familiar loss updates the token/position embeddings, decoder stack, and vocabulary prediction mapping; tied parameters are shared rather than separately counted. Save learned weights and keep their matching tokenizer/configuration. A checkpoint is not a list of contextual vectors for these three sentences, nor an explicit database of answers. Learned parameters can nevertheless memorize training text. Do not imply that saving weights prevents memorization.
The original 2018 GPT work explicitly followed LM pretraining with supervised adaptation. Thus decoder pretraining is relevant to understanding tasks as well as continuation. Pretraining describes a stage in a reuse workflow; autoregressive describes a prediction structure. Transition: “With the same text, how does this recipe’s supervision differ from BERT’s?”

Familiar loss, shown for this window. Same corpus does not mean the same learning signal—or a guaranteed winner.


Example-based adaptation of Berkeley’s matched MLM/causal diagrams, PDF pp. 36 and 58; Stanford CS224N, PDF p. 31. Two BERT targets are illustrative, not a 15% sample. Boundary tokens omitted; the first word is supplied as context.


TIME: 4 minutes. Keep the purpose on pretraining supervision. Read the targets, not another token-by-token generation trace. BERT’s MLM part has selected loss positions; GPT scores each eligible next-token target in its training window. Here there is no start token: the first word is context, so there are five scored targets. The final source token mat is the last label and needs no extra input position for this example. Boundary/padding conventions affect actual counts.
The displayed GPT input is processed with the already familiar causal mask. Although the complete prefix row is available to the training computation, a prediction cannot access later input positions. Do not reopen the attention matrix or the parallelism derivation. The equation is the known cross-entropy objective averaged over five targets; x2 is cat and x6 is mat. There is no new arithmetic task, and no new probability factorization to derive.
BERT’s unselected context states can still receive gradients; no direct loss at a position does not mean its representation is frozen. Selected-but-unchanged and randomly replaced positions also contribute to BERT’s MLM loss, even though this illustration uses MASK for both. NSP is omitted to isolate the token-level comparison, not silently removed from the historical BERT recipe.
More scored positions does not establish better representations. The available context and task difficulty also differ; fair comparisons need controlled data, model size, compute, and downstream evaluation. This slide reports no benchmark. Transition: “After the optimization stage, what does the saved base model give us?”
